recommendations: Do not change ThreadSnapshot field names, types, visibility, or the native create(Thread) signature without coordinating and updating the native VM implementation and running full VM builds.
Preserve the semantics that ThreadSnapshot.of may return null; ensure ThreadDumper and any consumers defensively handle absent snapshots and do not assume always-present data.

When modifying nested types used by snapshots, avoid non-static inner classes that implicitly capture the enclosing ThreadSnapshot; verify object retention and GC behavior if changing class structure.

Any change that affects serialization output (text layout, JSON keys, encoding, or MAX_BYTE_ARRAY_SIZE behavior) can break external consumers—treat output format as a de facto ABI and run diagnostic/client parsing tests.

Run the diagnostic and jcmd/jstack related tests (HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpThreads, Thread.dump_to_file, and relevant jtreg tests) as well as a full VM build when altering VM-facing contracts or file/output code.

src/java.base/share/classes/sun/security.description: This directory contains the Sun provider RSA key primitives and a KeyFactory implementation for RSA and RSASSA-PSS. It centralizes parsing/encoding (PKCS#1, PKCS#8, X.509), provider-specific key representations (CRT and non-CRT), and enforcement of RSA parameter policies (modulus sizes, exponent ranges) used throughout the JDK cryptography stack.
key_behaviors: Translate between generic JCA Key/KeySpec representations and provider-specific RSA key implementations
Parse and produce encoded key formats (PKCS#1, PKCS#8 for private keys; PKCS#1 and X.509 for public keys)
Validate RSA key parameters against configured security policy (modulus length, exponent constraints)
Choose and produce CRT vs non-CRT private key representations based on available components
Protect sensitive key material by zeroing temporary encoded byte arrays after use

insights.title: Centralized enforcement of RSA size and exponent rules
insights.problem: RSA keys created or translated here must obey global security policy (min/max modulus bits, exponent ranges).
insights.root_cause: RSAKeyFactory and key implementations are the choke points where various incoming encoded forms and Key/KeySpec inputs are accepted; inconsistent or missing checks would allow keys that violate expectations.
insights.solution: Any edits must preserve the validation logic and policy checks (modulus/exponent limits) and ensure they are applied consistently for all code paths that accept external encodings or generic Key objects.

insights.title: Multiple encodings and parsing paths (PKCS#1, PKCS#8, X.509)
insights.problem: There are multiple code paths that accept different encodings; divergence or regression in one parser/encoder will cause incompatibilities with other JDK components or external systems.
insights.root_cause: Each key class contains its own parsing and encoding utilities; operations such as engineGeneratePrivate/engineGeneratePublic and newKey use these routines.
insights.solution: When changing parsing/encoding behavior, ensure all encodings remain compatible, and update or coordinate all affected key classes and KeyFactory translation paths to keep encoding/decoding symmetrical.

insights.title: Zeroization and memory exposure risk
insights.problem: Temporary byte arrays holding private key encodings are zeroed in some places; inconsistent handling could leave secret material in memory.
insights.root_cause: Multiple locations create temporary encoded byte[]; omission of zeroing or refactoring that changes lifecycle risks leaving data un-cleared.
insights.solution: Maintain explicit zeroing semantics for temporary buffers that hold private key material and ensure any refactors preserve zeroization and do not introduce lingering references.

insights.title: CRT vs non-CRT key representation and AlgorithmId formation
insights.problem: Keys may need to be represented in CRT form or as simple modulus/exponent; choosing the wrong representation affects signing/decryption performance and produced encodings.
insights.root_cause: RSAPrivateCrtKeyImpl can return CRT or non-CRT representations depending on available components; AlgorithmId and encoding generation must reflect the chosen form.
insights.solution: Edits must respect when CRT components are present and preserve correct AlgorithmId/encoding generation corresponding to the stored representation.

insights.title: JCA exception types and provider translation semantics
insights.problem: KeyFactory must throw the correct JCA exceptions and produce the exact provider key types; API consumers rely on these behaviors.
insights.root_cause: engineTranslateKey, engineGeneratePublic, engineGeneratePrivate and other methods implement the KeyFactorySpi contract; changing thrown exception types or returned classes breaks callers and the provider contract.
insights.solution: Maintain the declared exception behavior and returned concrete key classes; any change that affects observable SPI behavior requires coordination with callers and tests.

key_files.why: Entry point for translation, generation and validation of RSA keys under the Sun provider; enforces policy and bridges generic JCA Keys/KeySpecs with provider key types.
Represents CRT private keys, parses PKCS#1/PKCS#8, and decides CRT vs non-CRT encoding — affects encoding symmetry and how private material is exposed/stored.
Non-CRT private key representation used when CRT components are absent; participates in encoding/decoding and AlgorithmId creation.
Public key representation and parser for X.509/PKCS#1 encodings; validates public exponent ranges used by policy enforcement.

construct_relationships: RSAKeyFactory.engineGeneratePublic/engineGeneratePrivate call RSAPublicKeyImpl and RSAPrivate(Crt)KeyImpl parsing/constructors to create provider-specific keys from encoded byte[] or KeySpecs.
RSAPrivateCrtKeyImpl.parsePKCS1 and RSAPublicKeyImpl.parsePKCS1 implement parallel PKCS#1 parsing logic that must agree on field ordering and validation rules.
RSAPrivateCrtKeyImpl can produce either CRT or non-CRT representations; RSAPrivateKeyImpl provides the non-CRT representation used when CRT components are missing.

RSAKeyFactory.toRSAKey and engineTranslateKey convert generic Key instances to the concrete RSAPublicKeyImpl/RSAPrivateKeyImpl/RSAPrivateCrtKeyImpl types expected by other Sun RSA components (e.g., signature and cipher implementations).
AlgorithmId/encoding creation in key implementations must produce encodings that RSAKeyFactory and other consumers can parse back reliably.
notable_relationships: This subtree is consumed by higher-level RSA implementations (RSASignature, RSACipher) and by JCA consumers via the KeyFactory SPI; changes affect runtime cryptographic operations.
Encodings produced here are part of the external interoperability contract (PKCS#1, PKCS#8, X.509) used across the JVM and by external tools; backward compatibility is important.
Validation behavior ties into global crypto policy (JDK security properties and potential provider-level policy enforcement); changes may interact with system-wide security settings.
Serialization and the concrete key classes are potentially visible to application code (Serializable keys); modifications can have cross-process compatibility implications.
recommendations: Preserve public SPI contracts: method signatures, exception types (InvalidKeyException, InvalidKeySpecException), and returned concrete key classes.
Do not weaken or remove modulus/exponent validation; ensure policy checks remain applied on all input paths (KeySpecs, encoded bytes, generic Key translations).
Retain zeroization semantics for temporary private key buffers; ensure any refactor continues to explicitly clear sensitive byte[] after use.

Keep encoding/decoding symmetric: any change to parser or encoder must be reflected across RSAPublicKeyImpl, RSAPrivateKeyImpl, RSAPrivateCrtKeyImpl and RSAKeyFactory so produced encodings remain parseable.

Run a full build and the JDK crypto-related tests (provider/key/cipher/signature jtreg/gtests and any RSA-specific test tiers) after edits; consider serialization compatibility and provider integration when altering key classes.
Consider thread-safety and immutability of key objects: avoid introducing mutable global state or exposing internal mutable arrays.

src/java.base/share/classes/sun/security.description: This package contains Sun/Oracle provider implementations and helpers for core Java security primitives: parsing and interning X.509 certificates/CRLs, PKCS#8 key handling (including a legacy password-based protector), and concrete DSA private key representations and supporting math routines. These classes sit in java.base and are on critical execution paths for certificate/key parsing, KeyStore I/O, and cryptographic operations, so correctness, binary compatibility, and performance constraints are important.
key_behaviors: Parse X.509 certificates, CRLs and CertPath objects from multiple encodings (DER, PEM/base64, PKCS#7) and return concrete X509 implementations
Intern and cache parsed certificates and CRLs to deduplicate identical encoded inputs across the runtime
Serialize/deserialize and expose ASN.1/PKCS#8 encodings for DSA private keys, and surface parameter values
Protect and recover PKCS#8 key bytes using a legacy password-derived XOR keystream with an integrity digest (used by legacy keystore storage)
Perform DSA-related low-level computations where multi-dimensional arrays and temporary buffers impact performance and allocation patterns

insights.title: Certificate/CRL interning introduces shared in-memory representatives
insights.problem: Interning and caching parsed X.509 objects means modifications to cached objects or changes to cache semantics can have widespread effects and risk memory retention/leaks or incorrect sharing semantics.
insights.root_cause: certCache and crlCache map encoded forms to shared X509 impl instances to reduce duplicates and allocations across consumers.
insights.solution: Treat cache semantics as part of the public behavior: any change must preserve identity/equals expectations, thread-safety, and ensure caches do not unintentionally retain unbounded memory (beware global strong references); consider effects on callers that depend on object identity or reference equality.

insights.title: Multi-format certificate/CRL parsing must preserve compatibility and enforce limits
insights.problem: X509Factory accepts DER, PEM, and PKCS#7 blobs; changing parsing behavior, limits (e.g. ENC_MAX_LENGTH), or stream reading semantics may break acceptance of valid external inputs or create DoS vectors.
insights.root_cause: Single central implementation handles multiple encodings and contains input-size and reading utilities (readFully) that gate parsing behavior.
insights.solution: Maintain strict, well-documented handling for PEM boundaries, PKCS#7 envelopes, and maximum encoded lengths; ensure stream-reading semantics and error handling remain compatible and defend against pathological large inputs.

insights.title: Legacy key protector encodes a proprietary format used by keystores
insights.problem: KeyProtector implements a non-standard, password-derived XOR scheme producing EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo blobs; any change to format, digest algorithm, or structure will break reading/writing of existing keystores and tooling that expects this legacy format.
insights.root_cause: The protector is a proprietary/exportable algorithm that derives a keystream from password+salt and embeds an integrity digest; consumers persist those blobs externally.
insights.solution: Preserve exact serialized format and integrity checks when modifying related code paths; treat the protector format as stable public artifact. When handling recover(), validate integrity behavior exactly and guard against malformed inputs.

insights.title: DSA private key ASN.1 encoding and parameter exposure must be exact
insights.problem: DSAPrivateKey constructs and exposes ASN.1/PKCS#8 encodings and DSA parameters; small changes to encoding order, OID selection, or parameter derivation affect signature verification and interoperability.
insights.root_cause: Concrete implementation marshals/unmarshals private values and parameters from AlgorithmIdentifier or stored fields, and callers rely on the produced canonical encoded form.
insights.solution: Preserve canonical ASN.1 encoding, OIDs and parameter handling; ensure getEncoded()/getParams() semantics remain consistent and that any parsing tolerates expected legacy variants without altering the emitted encodings.

insights.title: Multi-dimensional array allocation patterns are performance-sensitive
insights.problem: Some DSA/math routines allocate many multi-dimensional temporary arrays (e.g., new int[a][b]) which can be inefficient and GC-heavy on hot paths.
insights.root_cause: Use of nested array allocations and temporary objects for intermediate math causes frequent allocations and potential cache inefficiency.
insights.solution: When editing numeric/math code, respect allocation patterns and benchmarking; avoid introducing changes that increase transient allocation pressure or alter the lifetimes/size of temporary buffers on cryptographic hot paths.

key_files.why: Central CertificateFactorySpi implementation that parses DER/PEM/PKCS#7 certs/CRLs and manages the interning/caching layer used across the runtime.
Implements a legacy password-based protector for PKCS#8 keys; serialized format and integrity behavior are relied on by keystore persistence and tooling.
Concrete DSA private key representation that constructs and exposes ASN.1/PKCS#8 encodings and parameter accessors used by crypto operations and keystore code.
Contains DSA-related numerical routines where allocation patterns and temporary buffers have measurable performance and GC effects on crypto operations.

construct_relationships: X509Factory parses encoded certificate and CRL byte streams and produces X509CertImpl/X509CRLImpl instances, then interns those instances in certCache/crlCache for reuse.
KeyProtector.protect() and recover() operate on PKCS#8 encoded key bytes (EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo), which may encapsulate DSAPrivateKey encodings produced/consumed by DSAPrivateKey.
DSAPrivateKey produces and parses ASN.1 and PKCS#8 encodings that upstream code (keystore IO, KeyProtector, and signature subsystems) depend upon for serialization and deserialization.
ML_DSA provides low-level numeric operations used by DSA implementations; its allocation/temporary buffer behavior affects performance of DSA key operations and any code paths that use DSAPrivateKey.
notable_relationships: This subtree is in java.base and is used broadly by KeyStore implementations, JSSE/TLS stacks, certificate validation/path-building, and any code that reads or writes PKCS#8 or X.509 artifacts — edits can have cross-cutting runtime effects.

Serialized formats produced here (X.509 encodings, EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo produced by KeyProtector, PKCS#8 encodings) are persistent/portable artifacts consumed outside this package (disk keystores, network protocols), so changes affect interoperability.

ASN.1 parsing/encoding behavior ties into other sun.security.util classes and common security APIs; modifications may require coordinating with other security provider components and conformance tests.
Caching/interning choices affect memory/profile characteristics of long-running JVMs and can interact with multi-threaded certificate loading and validation in other packages.
recommendations: Preserve wire/serialized formats (ASN.1, PKCS#7, PEM boundaries, EncryptedPrivateKeyInfo structure) and constants (e.g., size limits) unless a coordinated compatibility strategy and tests are updated.
Respect caching/interning semantics: maintain thread-safety, identity/equals expectations, and be cautious of introducing strong global references that could cause memory leaks.

When changing parsing or stream-reading logic, validate behavior against a wide set of real-world DER/PEM/PKCS#7 inputs and ensure robust handling of large or malformed inputs; run the certificate/key JTReg tests and any interoperability suites.
For KeyProtector and keystore-related behavior, ensure exact integrity validation and format preservation; recognize these blobs are persisted externally and relied upon by existing keystores.

Any changes to math/numeric routines must consider allocation and GC pressure; run performance and memory benchmarks for crypto hot paths (DSA signing/verification and key operations) to detect regressions.

src/java.base/share/classes/jdk/internal.description: This package contains low-level, performance-sensitive utilities used by the java.base runtime: very small primitives for converting numeric values to ASCII/byte representations (hex and decimal) and helpers that compose exception messages while respecting security/sensitivity policies. These classes are part of the core runtime support and matter because they are used pervasively by formatting/IO code paths and must preserve performance, encoding semantics, and security constraints.
key_behaviors: Provide precomputed, immutable lookup tables and tiny APIs to convert numeric primitives (bytes, ints, longs) into ASCII hex/decimal byte or char sequences with minimal per-call work.
Render digits directly into Latin-1 (byte) or UTF-16 (char) buffers using unchecked/unsafe writes to avoid bounds checks and allocate/scoped temporary objects.
Compose and filter exception messages that may contain socket, jar, or user-identifying information according to runtime security policy (sensitive-info gating).
Expose compact, deterministic packed representations (e.g., two ASCII hex chars in a short) that callers expect to consume in a particular byte/order layout.

insights.title: Precomputed tables and unchecked buffer writes optimize hot paths
insights.problem: Decimal and hex conversion routines are used in hot code paths and must avoid per-call arithmetic and bounds checks.
insights.root_cause: Per-call computation and Java bounds checks introduce measurable overhead; performance code therefore precomputes digit pairs and uses Unsafe-based unchecked writes.
insights.solution: Maintain precomputed DIGITS tables and unchecked buffer writing patterns; any edits must preserve immutability, layout, and the unchecked write semantics or provide equivalent zero-cost alternatives. Changes that insert checks or allocate temporaries risk regressing runtime performance.

insights.title: Packed character representations and endianness/encoding assumptions
insights.problem: HexDigits packs two ASCII characters into a Java short in a specific little-endian byte order and DecimalDigits writes into Latin1/UTF-16 buffers; callers depend on these exact encodings and layouts.
insights.root_cause: The code encodes characters into primitive containers (short[], byte[], char[]) and uses direct memory writes; implicit assumptions about ordering and the target buffer encoding must hold across changes.
insights.solution: Preserve the exact packing order and buffer-encoding conventions (Latin-1 vs UTF-16) when modifying code. Any change to packing or write order requires coordinated updates to all consumers and careful consideration of platform/JSR-51 semantics.

insights.title: Use of Unsafe and unchecked APIs introduces coupling to VM behaviour
insights.problem: Unchecked get/put methods rely on Unsafe or internal mechanisms; improper changes can cause memory corruption, security holes, or crashes.
insights.root_cause: Direct memory writes bypass Java safety checks and assume correct buffer sizes and alignment provided by callers.
insights.solution: Treat Unsafe-based routines as low-level primitives that must not add or remove implicit preconditions. Maintain documented contract for buffer length and alignment expectations; any co-change must ensure callers still satisfy those contracts. Validate via native/regression tests when altering these paths.

insights.title: Exception message composition must honor sensitive-info policy
insights.problem: Exceptions may include socket/jar/user details which could leak sensitive data if policies are not enforced correctly.
insights.root_cause: Conditional augmentation of exception messages depends on runtime security checks and policy flags; mistakes may inadvertently expose sensitive attributes.
insights.solution: Any edits to message composition or filtering must preserve the policy checks and gating behavior (SensitiveInfo categories). Ensure changes keep the same decision points and that unit/IT tests for message content under different security configurations are run.

insights.title: Internal utilities are referenced broadly inside java.base and must remain stable
insights.problem: Although package-private/internal, these utilities are widely used by other core classes; changing signatures, contracts, or semantics can have broad impact.
insights.root_cause: Other core modules/components rely on microbehavior (packing, return types, unchecked semantics).
insights.solution: Any change must consider downstream callers within java.base and the HotSpot/native layers. Maintain ABI-like stability of method semantics, exception behavior, and data layout; update consumers in concert if semantics must change.

key_files.why: Provides the precomputed mapping and the primitive API to convert a single byte into two ASCII hex characters packed into a short — a tiny, high-frequency primitive used in formatting/serialization hotspots.

Contains the performance-critical routines for integer/long to ASCII decimal rendering, including buffer-size calculations and unchecked Latin-1/UTF-16 writes; central to numeric-to-string conversions in the runtime.
Encapsulates logic to build exception messages with sensitive-info awareness and to produce enhanced IOExceptions when allowed — affects many IO and networking failure flows.

construct_relationships: HexDigits provides a compact mapping (byte -> packed short with two ASCII hex chars) that higher-level formatting code can consume to write hex output rapidly.

DecimalDigits exposes DIGITS tables and unchecked getChars/putPair helpers to write decimal ASCII into Latin-1 or UTF-16 buffers; callers rely on its stringSize calculations to allocate or position writes without further bounds checking.
Exceptions defines SensitiveInfo categories and filtering helpers that callers in IO/networking paths use to decide whether to append socket/jar/user details to IOException messages.
notable_relationships: These utilities are in java.base and therefore are downstream-facing for virtually all other JDK modules; changes can affect core library formatting, logging, IO, and native interop.

DecimalDigits' use of Unsafe/unchecked writing ties into VM-level guarantees about memory model and may interact with HotSpot behaviors; changing write semantics or alignment could surface in native tests.

Exceptions' behavior is coupled to runtime security configuration and possibly to system properties or SecurityManager-like facilities; behavior changes affect diagnostic output across the platform and tests that assert exception message contents.
recommendations: Preserve existing method contracts: keep return types, packing order, and encoding conventions (Latin-1 vs UTF-16). If semantics must change, update all callers in the same change set.
Do not introduce runtime bounds checks or additional allocations in these hot-path routines without benchmarking — performance regressions are critical.
When touching Unsafe-using code, validate with low-level/native and jtreg tests to detect memory-safety or platform-specific failures; run make images and test-tier1 (or equivalent CI suites).
When modifying Exceptions, ensure sensitive-info gating logic remains intact and exercise security-configured tests that verify message contents under allowed/forbidden conditions.
Be mindful that these classes live in java.base (core) — changes may require rebuilds of the platform image and broader coordination; run platform builds and regression suites after edits.

src/java.base/share/classes/java/util/co.description: This subtree contains core concurrent utilities that implement executor, completion, and structured-concurrency behaviors used throughout the JDK. It provides default ExecutorService implementations for task submission and aggregation, a CompletionService that hands back completed task Futures, and a concrete structured task scope which manages lifetime, joining, cancellation and owner-thread semantics for forked subtasks. These classes encode subtle semantics for wrapping tasks, propagating cancellation/interrupts, handling timeouts and enqueuing completion results that callers and subclasses depend upon.
key_behaviors: Wrapping submitted Runnable/Callable into RunnableFuture wrappers (defaulting to FutureTask) so submissions uniformly return Futures and can be cancelled.

Implementing invokeAny/invokeAll with coordination: submitting multiple tasks, waiting for first-success or all-results, enforcing timeouts, cancelling remaining tasks on completion or timeout, and aggregating exceptions or results.
Enqueuing completed task Futures into a completion queue for later retrieval (blocking via take or non-blocking via poll).

Forking subtasks within a scope, managing their threads/lifecycle, joining to collect results via a Joiner, and enforcing owner-thread-only operations and cancellation propagation (including timeouts).

insights.title: Coordinated cancellation must reach all outstanding tasks and optionally interrupt running threads
insights.problem: invokeAny/invokeAll and StructuredTaskScopeImpl rely on cancelling leftover tasks; incorrect cancellation can leave tasks running or leak threads.
insights.root_cause: Cancellation is implemented by iterating active Future/RunnableFuture objects and calling cancel(true/false) while relying on wrapped tasks and thread interrupt semantics to stop execution.
insights.solution: Any edits must preserve the current strategy of cancelling outstanding Futures and interrupting threads where the API intends it; ensure any new wrappers or changes to cancellation sequencing maintain the same visibility and ordering guarantees so that tasks are not left running or unobserved.

insights.title: Timeouts are implemented by coordinated waiting and deadline arithmetic across multiple tasks
insights.problem: invokeAny/invokeAll and structured scopes use elapsed-time calculations and timed waits. Small differences in time accounting can lead to surprising wait durations or failure to cancel promptly.
insights.root_cause: Timeout logic is spread across submission, timed polling, and cancellation code paths that compute remaining time and may re-check conditions after partial waits.
insights.solution: Preserve existing deadline arithmetic and ordering: compute remaining nanoseconds consistently, guard against negative remaining time, and ensure timed waits and subsequent cancellations are invoked exactly as before to avoid changing semantics.

insights.title: Task wrapper customization is an extension point (newTaskFor)
insights.problem: AbstractExecutorService exposes newTaskFor hooks used by submit/invoke implementations. Subclasses may override them to provide different RunnableFuture behavior.
insights.root_cause: Submit/invoke paths assume newTaskFor produces a RunnableFuture with expected cancel/get behavior; replacing it with wrappers that do not integrate with existing cancellation or completion queuing breaks higher-level logic.
insights.solution: When modifying code that constructs RunnableFuture instances or the points where they are enqueued, keep the contract of newTaskFor intact (behavioral expectations for cancel, isDone, get, and interrupt handling) so subclass overrides continue to interoperate correctly.

insights.title: Completed Futures must be reliably enqueued even on exception or cancellation
insights.problem: ExecutorCompletionService relies on QueueingFuture to place completed tasks into the completion queue. Missed enqueues or double-enqueues change retrieval semantics and can lead to lost notifications or blocked consumers.
insights.root_cause: Queueing occurs in task-completion hooks; changes to those hooks or to exception paths can alter whether or when enqueue is called.
insights.solution: Maintain the invariant that every finished task—successful, failed, or cancelled—results in at most one enqueue to the completion queue and that enqueue happens exactly once when the Future transitions to done.

insights.title: StructuredTaskScope enforces owner-thread semantics and thread lifecycle rules
insights.problem: StructuredTaskScopeImpl expects operations like join and fork to be invoked by the owner thread; violating this can cause race conditions, incorrect joins, or misapplied cancellations.
insights.root_cause: Enforcement and assumptions about single-owner operations are embedded in join/cancel/termination checks and in management of the ThreadFlock.
insights.solution: Any change touching scope lifecycle, join logic, or thread management must preserve owner-thread checks and ensure that thread-flocking, interruption, and joiner behavior remain deterministic and race-free under concurrent attempts to operate on the scope.

key_files.why: Core default implementations of ExecutorService submission, invokeAny/invokeAll, and the extension hook newTaskFor that other executors and callers depend on.
Implements CompletionService semantics: submission via an Executor and reliable enqueueing of completed Futures for consumers via take/poll.
Concrete structured-concurrency scope implementation that manages forking/joining subtasks, owner-thread constraints, timeout/cancellation behavior and thread lifecycle.

construct_relationships: AbstractExecutorService wraps Runnable/Callable into RunnableFuture (via newTaskFor) and uses those wrappers to implement submit, invokeAny, and invokeAll flows that coordinate submission, waiting and cancellation.
ExecutorCompletionService submits tasks via a provided Executor and relies on a QueueingFuture wrapper to enqueue completed Future instances into a BlockingQueue for take/poll retrieval.

StructuredTaskScopeImpl forks Callables as SubtaskImpl instances and coordinates their threads through a ThreadFlock and a Joiner to aggregate results; it enforces owner-thread semantics and triggers cancellation/interrupts on scope termination.

Cancellation flows connect across components: invokeAny/invokeAll logic cancels outstanding RunnableFutures produced by newTaskFor; ExecutorCompletionService depends on completed state transitions of those Futures to populate its completion queue.
notable_relationships: Public APIs used here (Executor, ExecutorService, CompletionService, Callable, Future, RunnableFuture) are widely referenced across the JDK; changes will affect any callers and existing subclass overrides in other modules.

StructuredTaskScopeImpl introduces structured-concurrency semantics that interact with Thread/interrupt behavior and may be used by higher-level frameworks—maintain compatibility with Thread interruption and security policies.
Timeouts, cancellation and interrupt semantics have downstream effects on code in other packages that rely on timely task termination (e.g., tests in test/jdk/java/util/concurrent and other modules).
Queueing and blocking behavior touches scheduler/queue implementations (BlockingQueue implementations elsewhere); changes could alter liveness or ordering seen by consumers.
recommendations: Do not change the observable public API semantics: submission behavior, Future contract (cancel/get/isDone), invokeAny/invokeAll and completion-queue semantics must remain consistent with existing behavior.

Preserve cancellation and interrupt propagation ordering and ensure outstanding tasks are cancelled when invokeAny/invokeAll or StructuredTaskScopeImpl instructs cancellation; verify both future.cancel() and thread interruption interactions.
Maintain the newTaskFor extension contract so existing subclasses that override it continue to function; any alterations to wrapper creation must interoperate with cancel/get semantics.
When modifying timeout or waiting logic, preserve deadline arithmetic and negative-remaining-time handling to avoid changing wait durations or prematurely cancelling tasks.
Ensure QueueingFuture enqueueing invariants: each completed task transitions to done and is enqueued exactly once; changes must not introduce missed or duplicate enqueues.
Respect owner-thread checks and lifecycle rules in StructuredTaskScopeImpl; changes that relax or change these checks require careful reasoning about races and join/cancel behavior.

Run concurrency-focused regressions and the relevant jtreg tests (test/jdk/java/util/concurrent and structured-concurrency tests) plus threaded stress tests after edits to detect regressions in liveness, ordering, or cancellation.

src/java.base/share/classes/jdk/internal.description: This package contains low-level, VM-facing utilities for class data sharing (CDS) and specialized thread-local facilities tied to platform/carrier threads and their termination. It provides Java-side state, orchestration and helpers that the VM and tooling rely on when dumping/using shared archives, and it provides thread-local storage semantics and termination notifications that are implemented via SharedSecrets/JavaLangAccess. These classes are critical for correct VM/JVM-tooling interaction, resource lifecycle management, and preserving invariants across thread and classloader boundaries.
key_behaviors: Maintain and report global CDS state (dump vs use) and coordinate archive dump operations that involve both Java-level orchestration and native VM actions.
Dump shared archives and initialize archived static fields, including keeping referenced objects alive during static archive creation and handling classes not yet registered with the VM.
Generate holder classes used by dynamically-created lambda forms to be placed into shared archives and/or used at runtime.
Provide thread-local storage semantics bound to the underlying carrier/platform thread rather than the virtual thread, delegating actual storage access via SharedSecrets/JavaLangAccess.
Register and invoke thread termination callbacks for cleanup of native resources held by thread-local entries when a platform/carrier thread terminates.

insights.title: Java-side state mirrors VM dump/use lifecycle
insights.problem: Java code must remain consistent with native VM expectations about whether an archive is being dumped or used; mismatches can corrupt archives or lead to incorrect initialization of statics.
insights.root_cause: CDS state and operations span both Java and native code; Java-level flags and helpers are referenced by tooling and native code paths.
insights.solution: Treat the Java flags and dump routines as part of a contract with the VM: any edits must preserve semantics, synchronization and visibility so native code and tooling continue to observe correct CDS state.

insights.title: Keeping objects alive during static archive dumping
insights.problem: Objects referenced during archive dumping must not be GC-collected or otherwise released until dump completes, else archive contents will be invalid.
insights.root_cause: Archive-dump logic runs across Java and native boundaries; temporary live sets need explicit retention during the dump window.
insights.solution: Ensure retention helpers and any collections used to keep objects alive are reliable, visible to GC appropriately, and correctly cleared only after the native dump completes.

insights.title: Handling unregistered classes during CDS operations
insights.problem: Classes not registered with the VM at dump time (or during initialization from an archive) need special handling; failure results in unresolved references or classloading errors at runtime.
insights.root_cause: Archive dumping and initialization interact with classloader state and VM class registration paths.
insights.solution: Maintain careful coordination between generate/initialize helpers and classloader/VM registration semantics; preserve existing protocols for marking/registering or deferring classes.

insights.title: Thread-safe semantics for global flags and registries
insights.problem: Race conditions on CDS flags or on registration/unregistration of terminating thread-locals can lead to missed callbacks, double-free of native resources, or incorrect archive state.
insights.root_cause: These constructs are accessed from multiple threads and from native callbacks tied to VM lifecycle events.
insights.solution: Preserve synchronization behavior, atomicity and ordering; ensure any changes maintain visibility guarantees between threads and across Java/native boundaries.

insights.title: Carrier thread storage and termination rely on JLA bridge
insights.problem: The CarrierThreadLocal and TerminatingThreadLocal classes delegate actual storage and termination notifications to implementations accessed via SharedSecrets/JavaLangAccess; changes breakage here will disable carrier-thread semantics and cleanup.
insights.root_cause: The runtime-level carrier-thread behavior is implemented outside these Java classes; they are wrappers that rely on a separate internal API.
insights.solution: Keep method signatures, expected behaviors and registration protocols intact when editing; coordinate with SharedSecrets/JLA consumers/providers if changing contracts.

insights.title: Termination callbacks must be reliably invoked
insights.problem: If termination registry semantics change or unregistration is incorrect, native resources may leak or be freed at the wrong time.
insights.root_cause: TerminatingThreadLocal implements a registry of callbacks invoked on platform-thread termination; these callbacks are essential to free native resources bound to thread-local state.
insights.solution: Any modification must preserve registration/unregistration invariants and guarantee callbacks are invoked exactly when the VM signals a carrier/thread termination event.

key_files.why: Core orchestration and state for Class Data Sharing: dump/use flags, archive dumping, initialization of archived statics, lambda-form holder generation, and unregistered class handling — central VM-tooling contract.
Defines carrier-thread-bound thread-local semantics and delegates storage access via SharedSecrets/JavaLangAccess — the bridge for carrier-thread storage.
Extends carrier-thread-local semantics with a registry and termination callbacks used to free native resources when platform/carrier threads terminate — important for resource lifecycle.

construct_relationships: TerminatingThreadLocal extends CarrierThreadLocal and reuses its carrier-thread storage delegation while adding a registry of termination callbacks.

CarrierThreadLocal delegates get/set/remove storage operations to an implementation obtained via SharedSecrets -> JavaLangAccess; thus CarrierThreadLocal depends on the JLA bridge for actual storage behavior.

CDS utilities (CDS.java) manage global dump/use state and perform operations that require keeping Java objects alive and coordinating with native VM dump routines (native hooks called from Java routines).

CDS.generateLambdaFormHolderClasses produces class definitions that must be compatible with classloader and VM registration semantics used by initializeFromArchive and UnregisteredClassLoader handling.
notable_relationships: These classes form a Java-side contract with the native VM (HotSpot) and tooling: any behavioral or API changes may require corresponding native (C/C++) changes or adjustments in SharedSecrets/JLA providers.

CarrierThreadLocal and TerminatingThreadLocal rely on SharedSecrets/JavaLangAccess in the java.lang package; changes may affect or be affected by other modules that provide the JLA implementation (native runtime or platform-specific code).

CDS interactions touch classloading, java.lang.invoke (lambda forms), and archive format semantics — downstream consumers include the HotSpot CDS machinery, build tooling that creates archives, and runtime image initialization code.

Tests and CI (jtreg, HotSpot tests) likely exercise archive dumping, lambda holder generation and thread termination cleanup; failures here can manifest as VM startup, class initialization, or native resource leaks.
recommendations: Preserve existing public/private signatures and behaviors that are observed by native code and SharedSecrets/JLA providers; changing method signatures or expected side-effects may break native integrations.
Maintain thread-safety and atomic visibility for global flags, registries and any collections used for retention during dump; ensure synchronization semantics are not weakened.

When editing CDS-related logic, validate against native expectations: coordinate with HotSpot/native code owners if you change semantics that cross the Java/native boundary and run full builds that include native VM components.

For CarrierThreadLocal/TerminatingThreadLocal edits, verify interaction with SharedSecrets/JavaLangAccess remains correct; ensure registration/unregistration semantics for termination callbacks are preserved to avoid native resource leaks.

Run the appropriate test suites after changes: full JDK build (make images), JTReg tests that exercise CDS and startup, and VM/native tests that cover class registration and thread termination behavior.

src/java.desktop/unix/classes/sun/awt/sc.description: This folder implements Unix-specific screencast and remote-desktop integration for the Java desktop module. It bridges Java code with the XDG Desktop Portal / PipeWire native stack, manages persistent restore tokens and secure storage, and chooses the appropriate portal method based on the runtime desktop environment so that screenshots and remote input can be performed across Wayland / X11 desktops.
key_behaviors: Selecting the appropriate capture/input delivery method at runtime (x11 vs dbus screencast vs dbus remote-desktop) based on environment detection (Wayland/X11, GNOME version, system properties).
Loading native libraries and invoking native capture/pipewire code to obtain RGB pixel arrays and to forward remote-desktop input events.
Managing screencast session lifecycle including session auto-close timers and persistent restore tokens that permit future reconnection without user re-authorization.
Persisting and loading tokens and allowed screen bounds from a user properties file, watching that file for external changes, and pruning malformed entries.
Translating Java-level remote input calls (mouse move, button, key) into native calls while using stored tokens to authenticate/authorize those actions.

insights.title: Tight coupling to native PipeWire / XDG portal libraries
insights.problem: ScreencastHelper relies on native library loading and native implementations for both capture and remote input; failures at load-time or API mismatches will break runtime functionality.
insights.root_cause: Platform-dependent native code and JNI boundaries whose behavior and ABI depend on installed portal/pipewire versions and distribution packaging.
insights.solution: Treat native library loading and all native-call entry points as brittle: preserve expected JNI signatures, check loading/error paths, and ensure any Java-level changes maintain the contract with native implementations; validate behavior on target desktop environments where portal/pipewire differ.

insights.title: Session timers and watcher threads affect lifecycle and resource cleanup
insights.problem: Auto-close timers for sessions and the TokenStorage file watcher introduce background activity that can race with shutdown, token updates, and native session teardown.
insights.root_cause: Asynchronous threads and scheduled tasks managing sessions and file-watching without global coordination points across classes.
insights.solution: Coordinate any change with existing lifecycle hooks: preserve timer semantics and ensure clean shutdown ordering; when modifying behavior, validate thread-safety and avoid leaks or races between token updates, native session termination, and file watcher actions.

insights.title: Persistent tokens stored in user properties must be secured and robustly handled
insights.problem: Token persistence file is sensitive and can be malformed, externally modified, or copied from legacy locations; incorrect permissions or parsing errors can expose tokens or fail restores.
insights.root_cause: Tokens are stored on disk and TokenStorage must both enforce secure permissions and tolerate (and prune) malformed records while supporting migration from secondary locations.
insights.solution: Maintain strict file permission handling, atomic write/update semantics, and robust parsing with pruning; any change must keep the same on-disk token format or provide a compatible migration path and preserve security controls (file mode/ownership).

insights.title: Capture method selection depends on environment detection heuristics
insights.problem: XdgDesktopPortal determines method using runtime environment signals (Wayland vs X11, GNOME version, system properties). Mistakes here may pick unsupported flows causing runtime errors.
insights.root_cause: Heuristic-based selection and multiple possible portal implementations across distributions and desktop versions.
insights.solution: When modifying selection logic or code paths that depend on it, ensure that decisions remain conservative and that downstream code (ScreencastHelper/native) can handle chosen modes; ensure tests or runtime checks exist for Wayland/X11 and different GNOME versions.

key_files.why: Primary integration point that loads native libraries, manages capture sessions, retrieves pixel arrays, and sends remote-desktop input events; the main place where Java meets native PipeWire/XDG portal code.
Manages persistent restore tokens, secure on-disk storage, and a watcher thread for external updates — changes here affect token lifecycle and security for restored screencast sessions.
Encapsulates runtime detection and selection of the portal/capture method; influences which native and Java code paths in ScreencastHelper are exercised at runtime.

construct_relationships: ScreencastHelper calls native implementations (loadPipewire, getRGBPixelsImpl, remoteDesktop*Impl) to perform screen capture and remote input.
ScreencastHelper obtains and uses restore tokens persisted by TokenStorage to authenticate or authorize remote-desktop sessions and to forward remote input.
TokenStorage runs a WatcherThread to detect external changes to the token properties file and exposes getTokens for ScreencastHelper to read updated tokens.
ScreencastHelper consults XdgDesktopPortal.getMethod / isRemoteDesktop / isScreencast to decide which capture or input mechanism to use and which native flows to invoke.
notable_relationships: This code depends on external system components (xdg-desktop-portal, PipeWire, DBus, Wayland/X11 compositors) and on matching native libraries built for those components; runtime behavior can vary by distribution and desktop environment.
Persistent token files are user-local and interact with OS file permissions and possibly distribution migration paths; any change may affect cross-session restore across upgrades.
Tests and integrations exercising these classes require system-level capabilities and services (DBus, PipeWire) and therefore are likely to be integration/system tests rather than pure unit tests.
recommendations: When editing methods that call native code, preserve JNI method signatures and loading semantics; verify on-target desktop environments where the native side is expected to be present.
Respect and preserve the session lifecycle semantics: auto-close timers, session teardown, and ordering between token updates and native session shutdown to avoid races and leaks.
Maintain TokenStorage on-disk format, secure permission handling, atomic write semantics, and the watcher behavior; ensure parsing remains tolerant of malformed records and continues pruning them.
If changing XdgDesktopPortal selection logic, validate across Wayland and X11, and across GNOME versions or system property overrides to avoid enabling unsupported native flows.

Run integration tests that exercise file-watcher behavior and token restore flows, and perform runtime tests on systems with xdg-desktop-portal / PipeWire available; verify file permissions and native library load failures are handled gracefully.

src/java.desktop/unix/classes/sun/java2d.description: This folder implements the GLX/OpenGL-backed pieces of the Java2D pipeline for Unix/X11: it supplies a GLX-aware GraphicsConfig, concrete GLX SurfaceData variants (window and offscreen), and a VolatileSurfaceManager that decides and instantiates GLX-accelerated volatile images. These classes bridge Java2D SurfaceData/VolatileImage semantics with native GLX operations (via JNI/native libs) to provide accelerated drawing, buffer swapping and fallback behavior when GL capabilities are absent or allocation fails.
key_behaviors: Probe and initialize native GLX/OpenGL configuration and capabilities per X11 GraphicsConfig at startup or first use.
Create and manage GL-backed surfaces for windows and offscreen targets (FBOs, textures, backbuffers), exposing scale-aware bounds and restore semantics.
Decide at volatile-image allocation time whether to accelerate using GLX, instantiate appropriate GLXSurfaceData, and fall back to software if allocation or capability checks fail.
Perform buffer swap/flip operations and expose BufferCapabilities/ImageCapabilities consistent with underlying GLX double-buffering and vsync behavior.
Coordinate native GLX operation initialization (initOps) and ensure operations are usable from the Java2D rendering pipeline while respecting X11/GL threading constraints.

insights.title: Tight coupling with native GLX initialization
insights.problem: GLX functionality depends on explicit native initialization paths (initOps) and on information queried from GLX configs; incorrect ordering or signature mismatches will break accelerated surface creation and flips.
insights.root_cause: Java-side classes assume presence of properly initialized JNI/native GLX hooks and config probing results; changes to Java method signatures or initialization order are invisible to the native layer unless coordinated.
insights.solution: Treat native init calls and the contract they expose as part of the public behavior of these classes; any edits that change initialization sequences, method signatures, or expected capability flags must be coordinated with the native implementation and validated on target platforms.

insights.title: Allocation failures and safe fallback semantics
insights.problem: GL-backed surface allocation (FBOs/backbuffers/textures) can fail; without consistent fallback the rendering pipeline or volatile image lifecycle can enter invalid states.
insights.root_cause: GPU driver limits, GLX capability differences, or runtime resource exhaustion cause native allocation to fail; Java code must decide and create alternative SurfaceData or return null.
insights.solution: Maintain explicit handling for allocation failure paths: detect failed allocations, leave SurfaceData in a consistent state, trigger fallbacks to non-accelerated implementations, and ensure callers are prepared to handle null/alternative returns.

insights.title: X11/GL context and threading constraints
insights.problem: GLX and X11 have thread-affinity and context restrictions; invoking native GLX ops from the wrong thread or without serialization can cause race conditions or crashes.
insights.root_cause: Java2D rendering may occur on the AWT event thread or other worker threads, but GLX expects certain calls to be serialized or executed on a context-bound thread.
insights.solution: Preserve existing synchronization and context-binding assumptions: any edits must respect where and how initOps, surface creation, flips, and context activation happen, and must ensure safe use across Java threads and the AWT/EDT model.

insights.title: Heterogeneous GLX capability landscape
insights.problem: Different systems provide different GLX/OpenGL features (FBO support, double-buffering, vsync, scale factors), so a single code path cannot assume uniform capabilities.
insights.root_cause: Hardware drivers, GLX versions and server configurations vary across Unix environments.
insights.solution: Keep capability probing and per-config caching intact; edits should not remove or weaken capability checks, and must preserve code paths for both FBO-backed and backbuffer/texture-backed surfaces.

insights.title: Integration with Java2D SurfaceData/VolatileImage lifecycle
insights.problem: These classes participate in higher-level contracts (SurfaceData replacement/restore, VolatileSurfaceManager accelerationEnabled semantics, BufferCapabilities exposed to callers); breaking those contracts will disrupt callers across java.desktop.
insights.root_cause: SurfaceData and VolatileSurfaceManager semantics are consumed by many Java2D components and test suites; internal changes must preserve expected behaviors (e.g., restore notifications, contentsLost flags, buffer flips).
insights.solution: Respect and retain public behavioral contracts: ensure created SurfaceData implement required lifecycle callbacks, expose consistent capabilities, and trigger the same restore/contents-lost flows used by the Java2D framework.

key_files.why: Entry point that ties GLX capability probing to the Java GraphicsConfig abstraction and implements creation of GL-backed surfaces and buffer/flip semantics.
Concrete SurfaceData implementations for window and offscreen GLX-backed surfaces; encapsulates native operation initialization and the actual drawing/flip entry points used by Java2D.
Decision-maker for accelerating SunVolatileImage instances on GLX; handles runtime choices between FBO, backbuffer or software and governs fallback behavior.

construct_relationships: GLXGraphicsConfig extends X11GraphicsConfig and relies on GLX native probing to populate OGL capabilities and Buffer/ImageCapabilities returned to callers.
GLXGraphicsConfig delegates creation of GL-backed SurfaceData instances to GLXSurfaceData (via createData helpers) for window and offscreen targets.
GLXSurfaceData.initOps initializes JNI/native GLX operations that are consumed by GLXSurfaceData instances and by GLXGraphicsConfig during flips and buffer operations.

GLXVolatileSurfaceManager queries GLXGraphicsConfig capabilities and uses GLXSurfaceData factories to create accelerated volatile image backing (FBO or backbuffer); it also handles fallback to software when GLX allocation fails.

Higher-level Java2D components (SurfaceData consumers, VolatileImage lifecycle) interact with these classes through standard SurfaceData and VolatileSurfaceManager interfaces; these classes must present consistent behaviors to those callers.
notable_relationships: Depends on native (JNI) GLX/OpenGL bindings implemented in the platform-specific native image libraries (libawt/libj2d) — changes here may require corresponding native updates.
Couples with sun.java2d.x11/X11GraphicsConfig and other java.desktop classes that provide base X11 behaviors and the generic SurfaceData/VolatileImage contracts.
Downstream affects: Java2D rendering pipeline and any code that queries BufferCapabilities/ImageCapabilities (e.g., toolkit components, accelerated rendering paths).

Platform sensitivity: behavior is specific to Unix/X11 targets and must be validated on CI platforms exercising linux-x64 and other Unix variants (including low-level driver differences on environments like Alpine).
Test surface: affected by test/jdk/java2d jtreg tests and any integration tests that verify accelerated graphics, flips, vsync and volatile image restore semantics.
recommendations: Preserve native initialization ordering and JNI method signatures; coordinate any change that touches native-init or native-call sites with the native code owners and validate on actual Linux/X11 systems.
Do not remove or weaken capability probing: maintain per-config caching and fallback checks for FBO, backbuffer and vsync support.
Respect X11/GL threading and context-affinity: ensure calls that interact with GLX ops remain executed under the same threading/locking model as before.

Ensure all allocation failure paths leave SurfaceData and VolatileSurfaceManager state consistent and trigger the expected fallback and restore flows; verify callers handle null/alternative SurfaceData returns.
When editing these files, run platform-specific Java2D tests (jtreg java2d tests) and build on Linux/X11 targets to validate native interactions, buffer flip behavior and volatile image lifecycle.
If changing public behaviors (capabilities, buffer-flip semantics, lifecycle callbacks), review callers in other java.desktop packages and corresponding native code to avoid contract mismatches.

src/java.base/share/classes/sun/security.description: This package contains internal JDK representations and utilities for PKCS#8 private keys (RFC 5958). It provides parsing of DER-encoded PKCS#8 structures, canonical DER encoding generation (with caching), secure storage of raw private key material (including named-parameter keys), and serialization integration for provider-specific PrivateKey instantiation. These classes are critical for key import/export, KeyStore interactions, provider interoperability, and ensuring sensitive key material is handled securely at runtime.
key_behaviors: Parsing DER-encoded PKCS#8 v1 and v2 structures into an internal representation that preserves algorithm identifier, raw private-key octets, optional attributes, and optional public-key encoding.
Producing canonical DER PKCS#8 encodings and caching the generated encoding for subsequent calls to getEncoded/getEncodedInternal.
Yielding provider-specific PrivateKey instances by cooperating with the KeyFactory/provider layer (deferred conversion from raw encoding to runtime key object).
Secure lifecycle management of sensitive material: storing raw key bytes, zeroizing on destroy/clear, and exposing destroyed-state checks.
Serialization compatibility via writeReplace/KeyRep so that keys remain interoperable across serialization boundaries and JVM versions.

insights.title: In-memory raw key bytes must be explicitly cleared and destroyed
insights.problem: Private key raw bytes and cached encodings are sensitive and can remain in memory unless explicitly zeroized; improper changes can leave secrets accessible after intended destruction.
insights.root_cause: Design stores raw private-key octets and cached encoded forms as in-memory byte arrays and retains references until cleared or GC; default GC does not zero memory.
insights.solution: Respect and preserve explicit zeroization and destroyed-state semantics: when modifying constructors, fields, or caching, ensure clear/destroy logic zeroes byte arrays, clears cached encodings, flips isDestroyed flags, and avoids creating lingering copies in logs/exceptions. Consider concurrent access when clearing so callers cannot observe partial state.

insights.title: Encoded form is canonical and cached; cache coherence matters
insights.problem: Multiple callers rely on a canonical DER encoding; changes that alter encoding generation or caching behavior can break equality, serialization, provider KeyFactory compatibility, or KeyStore import/export.
insights.root_cause: PKCS#8 encodings are produced deterministically and cached by the object; callers (equals/hashCode/serialization/KeyFactory) depend on that stable representation and on the cache being consistent with the current internal state.
insights.solution: Any edits must preserve deterministic DER generation and keep cached encoding consistent with internal fields. If internal state mutability is introduced, ensure cache invalidation paths are well-defined and thread-safe so getEncoded and equals/hashCode remain stable and predictable.

insights.title: Provider conversion and serialization compatibility are fragile touchpoints
insights.problem: These classes act as bridges between raw PKCS#8 bytes and provider-specific PrivateKey implementations and also participate in Java serialization; incompatible changes can break KeyFactory translation, KeyStore behavior, and serialized-key compatibility across JVM versions.
insights.root_cause: writeReplace/KeyRep based serialization relies on exact encoded forms and algorithm identifiers; provider conversion depends on AlgorithmId/OID mapping and KeyFactory conventions outside this package.
insights.solution: Maintain exact semantics of algorithm identifier storage, public-key and attribute preservation, and the writeReplace/KeyRep contract. When changing representation or accessors, consider the downstream KeyFactory/provider mapping and serialization consumers to avoid breaking deserialization or provider lookup.

key_files.why: Central internal representation of PKCS#8 private keys: parsing, canonical encoding generation/caching, provider conversion points, equals/hashCode, clear/destroy and serialization integration.

Specialized representation for named-parameter private keys (e.g., X25519): stores raw bytes with NamedParameterSpec, provides parameter accessors and secure destruction behavior consistent with PKCS#8 handling.

construct_relationships: PKCS8Key represents parsed PKCS#8 structures (algorithm identifier, raw private-key octets, optional attributes/public key) and exposes getEncoded/getEncodedInternal used by serialization and provider conversion.

PKCS8Key exposes integration points that hand off encoded PKCS#8 data to KeyFactory/provider code to create concrete PrivateKey instances; serialization via writeReplace returns KeyRep built from the canonical encoding.

NamedPKCS8Key is a specialized PKCS#8-backed key representation for algorithms parameterized by a named parameter set; it shares the same secure-destruction and encoding semantics and provides parameter access through NamedParameterSpec while encapsulating raw key bytes.
notable_relationships: These classes interact closely with java.security.KeyFactory and provider implementations: modifications can affect provider-based instantiation of PrivateKey objects and KeyStore import/export flows.

The writeReplace/KeyRep serialization path ties these classes to java.io.ObjectInputStream/ObjectOutputStream consumers and to any persistence or remote-serialization consumers in the platform or applications.

Algorithm identifier handling and OID <-> algorithm/parameter mapping align with other sun.security.* components (e.g., AlgorithmId, ASN.1 utilities); changes may require coordination with those modules or tests that assume specific encoding formats.
JTReg/unit tests, KeyStore loading/saving, and cryptographic interoperability tests are downstream consumers that will detect regressions in parsing, encoding, or zeroization behavior.
recommendations: Preserve public and package-private contracts: do not change encoding format, serialization semantics (writeReplace/KeyRep), exposed accessors used by KeyFactory, or equals/hashCode behavior without coordinating downstream consumers.

Ensure any edits maintain explicit zeroization semantics: clear/destroy must zero out byte arrays, clear cached encoding, and set destroyed-state atomically/consistently; avoid creating transient copies of raw bytes in logs, exceptions or diagnostic messages.

Maintain deterministic DER generation and ensure cache consistency and thread-safety: if internal state can change, provide safe cache invalidation to keep getEncoded/getEncodedInternal stable for callers.

Run relevant test suites after changes: jtreg tests that exercise PKCS#8 parsing/serialization, KeyStore import/export tests, provider KeyFactory tests, and serialization compatibility tests to detect regressions.

Be mindful of interactions with AlgorithmId/OID mapping and provider code in other sun.security packages; coordinate changes that affect algorithm identifiers, parameter encoding, or public-key inclusion so provider lookups continue to succeed.

test/hotspot/jtreg/runtime/cds/appcds/ao.description: This folder contains jtreg tests that exercise Application CDS (AppCDS) AOT code caching behavior in HotSpot. The tests focus on combinations of AOT-related diagnostic JVM flags and on behavior when compressed references (narrow oops) are present; they rely on VM log output and specific runtime flag interactions, so they are sensitive to VM logging format and platform/address representations.
key_behaviors: Launch JVM with specific AppCDS/AOT diagnostic flags and observe runtime behavior/diagnostics
Parse HotSpot log output to extract VM-internal values (e.g. narrow_oop_base) and assert expectations
Validate interactions between AOT code caching, AppCDS snapshots, and compressed-oop addressing under test harness (jtreg)

insights.title: Regex for narrow_oop_base failed on hex addresses
insights.problem: A test pattern expected decimal digits when extracting narrow_oop_base from VM logs, but the VM emitted a hexadecimal address, causing parsing to fail and the test to be brittle.
insights.root_cause: Test-side parsing assumed a specific numeric format rather than matching the address format actually produced by the VM build/platform/logging configuration.
insights.solution: Treat VM log output as platform- and build-dependent; parsing should tolerate alternate numeric formats (hex/decimal) or rely on stable, structured diagnostics. When changing tests or VM logging, validate parsing across platforms and builds to avoid flaky failures.

insights.title: Tests depend on specific AOT/AppCDS diagnostic flags and their interactions
insights.problem: Tests assert behavior that arises only for particular combinations of JVM diagnostic flags and AppCDS/AOT code cache state, making them sensitive to flag semantics and default settings.
insights.root_cause: Tight coupling between test expectations and HotSpot flag semantics (including default values and interactions) and reliance on the jtreg invocation environment.
insights.solution: Any edits must respect that tests will be executed under jtreg with explicit JVM flags; maintain clarity about which flags are required. When altering tests or surrounding infrastructure, ensure test invocations include the same flags and re-run jtreg across relevant configurations to catch regressions.

insights.title: Address/representation and compressed-oop behavior vary by platform/build
insights.problem: Tests that inspect compressed-oop internals or memory base values can behave differently across architectures, address-widths, or build-time logging formats.
insights.root_cause: Differences in pointer/address formatting (hex vs decimal), presence/absence of compressed oops, and VM logging configuration across platforms/build variants.
insights.solution: When modifying tests or code that produces diagnostic output, verify behavior on multiple target platforms and build variants (e.g., compressed-oops enabled/disabled) and ensure test expectations document any platform-specific assumptions.

key_files.why: Java jtreg test that exercises permutations of AOT/AppCDS diagnostic JVM flags and acts as an entrypoint for validating flag-driven AOT behaviors.
Test that inspects compressed-oop-related VM diagnostics (narrow_oop_base) by parsing VM log output; demonstrates fragile log-parsing dependency and platform sensitivity.

construct_relationships: AOTCodeFlags.main invokes JVM runs under jtreg with specific AppCDS/AOT diagnostic flags to trigger and validate AOT code caching behavior.
AOTCodeCompressedOopsTest executes the JVM with compressed-oop related configuration and parses HotSpot diagnostic logs to extract narrow_oop_base for assertions.
Both tests depend on the jtreg harness to set up JVM invocation, capture stdout/stderr, and report pass/fail outcomes based on parsed diagnostics and exit codes.
notable_relationships: These tests depend on HotSpot's logging/diagnostic output format and the AppCDS/AOT implementation in the native VM (src/hotspot). Changes to VM log messages, formatting, or flag semantics upstream will directly affect these tests.

Behavior under test is sensitive to platform/architecture (pointer width, compressed-oop availability) and build variants; the jtreg execution environment and configure/build options (from the top-level build) influence test results.
The jtreg harness and its invocation (test runtime flags, environment) are an external dependency: modifications to jtreg usage in CI or local test runners may change how these tests must be invoked.
recommendations: Preserve test invocation flags and the expectation that jtreg will run the JVM with explicit AppCDS/AOT diagnostic options; when editing tests, confirm the exact JVM arguments used by jtreg.

Any change that affects VM diagnostic text or numeric formatting (addresses) must be validated because tests parse logs; ensure parsing logic tolerates hex and decimal address forms or that log text remains stable.
Run the relevant jtreg tests locally after edits across representative platforms/builds (especially with and without compressed oops) to catch platform-specific parsing or behavioral differences.

Avoid altering strings emitted by the VM logging subsystem without coordinating corresponding test updates; if VM messaging changes, update tests and re-run jtreg suites that depend on those messages.

Be aware of cross-cutting effects from HotSpot native changes (src/hotspot) and build/configure options that control compressed-oop and AppCDS behavior; verify tests under the same build configuration used by CI.

test/jdk/jdk/jfr/event/profiling.description: This folder contains jtreg integration tests that exercise Java Flight Recorder (JFR) profiling events (primarily CPUTimeSample and ExecutionSample), their throttling semantics, and full-stack trace capture. The tests coordinate background threads (including native-like busy loops and deep-recursion helpers), RecordingStream handlers, and thread/CPU-time measurement to validate VM sampling behaviour across timing thresholds and multiple recording lifecycles.
key_behaviors: Enable and configure JFR profiling event types (CPUTimeSample, ExecutionSample) via RecordingStream, then observe emitted events through registered event handlers or recording dumps.
Drive reproducible stack capture using a deterministic RecursiveMethods helper and a recursion-spawning thread; validate stack frame order, depth and truncation.
Trigger sampling by running busy threads (Java or native-like) to elicit CPU-time based samples; some tests call nativeMethod declarations to simulate or drive native workloads.
Measure and assert sampling rates and throttling using thread CPU-time (ThreadMXBean) rather than wall-clock time to reduce flakiness.
Create, close, and recreate RecordingStream instances to verify native sampling events survive multiple recording lifecycles and VM internal threshold transitions.

insights.title: Tests rely on timing/throttling thresholds and are sensitive to scheduling and system load
insights.problem: Some tests assume sampling/threshold timings (e.g., naked_short_sleep ~1000ms) and use wall-clock or throttle periods that can interact with OS scheduling, causing intermittent failures on loaded or slow machines.
insights.root_cause: JFR sampling behavior and VM internal thresholds interact with external factors (OS sleep behavior, CPU scheduling, variable machine load) causing non-deterministic sampling intervals when measured by wall-clock.
insights.solution: Prefer CPU-time based measurements where available (already used in throttling tests) and preserve explicit timing logic; any edits must preserve or carefully adjust timing controls, and maintain test resilience strategies already present.

insights.title: Several tests depend on native-like busy loops or nativeMethod stubs
insights.problem: Native-method declarations and native workload semantics are relied on to produce sampling events; missing or mismatched native implementations will break tests.
insights.root_cause: Tests declare native methods or expect native-like CPU consumption behavior; the implementation may live outside these Java files (test native libraries, harness infrastructure), so Java test changes alone can expose mismatches.
insights.solution: Treat nativeMethod declarations and any assumptions about native loop behavior as externally coupled; changes to method signatures, packages, or thread lifecycle must be coordinated with native harnesses and verified in environments that provide the native implementations.

insights.title: Full-stack trace validations depend on deterministic recursion and thread identities
insights.problem: The BaseTestFullStackTrace harness asserts specific frame orders, depths, and truncation behavior using the RecursiveMethods helper and sampled thread naming; non-deterministic stack frames or altered helper structure will invalidate assertions.
insights.root_cause: Tests expect exact stack shapes produced by a fixed sequence of Java methods; any reordering, inlining, or removal of methods (or changes to compilation/special-casing) affects captured traces.
insights.solution: Preserve the RecursiveMethods call sequence, method names, and the way threads are started/identified; be mindful of JVM optimizations that can change stack shape and ensure test JVM flags or build modes maintain comparability.

insights.title: Multiple RecordingStream creations and closures are validated
insights.problem: Tests verify that native sampling and event delivery continue after closing and reopening RecordingStream instances; improper resource or lifecycle handling can lead to false negatives.
insights.root_cause: RecordingStream close/open interacts with VM internals that manage native sampling facilities; tests rely on correct teardown and reinitialization semantics.
insights.solution: When modifying tests or related APIs, ensure RecordingStream lifecycle semantics are preserved; tests assume closing a stream fully stops delivery for that stream and that new streams start fresh sampling.

key_files.why: Reusable harness that orchestrates recordings, collects profiling events and asserts full-stack trace semantics — central to full-stack tests.
Validates CPUTimeSample throttling using ThreadMXBean-based CPU-time measurement; encodes resilience strategies against wall-clock variability.
Demonstrates native workload sampling behavior and relies on native-like busy loops / nativeMethod declarations to trigger VM sampling.
Parameterizes scenarios for both CPUTimeSample and ExecutionSample with specific attribute values to exercise VM sleep/throttle thresholds.
Provides the deterministic deep-recursion call chains used by full-stack validation tests; changes here affect stack-shape assertions.

construct_relationships: BaseTestFullStackTrace starts recursion threads that call RecursiveMethods to produce deterministic deep stacks and then opens RecordingStream to capture profiling events for validation.

Tests (TestCPUTimeSampleNative, TestCPUTimeSampleMultipleRecordings, TestCPUTimeSamplingLongPeriod, TestCPUTimeAndExecutionSample) enable specific JFR event types on RecordingStream and register handlers that stop background threads and close the recording upon observing events.

TestCPUTimeSampleThrottling configures CPUTimeSample event throttle attributes, uses ThreadMXBean to measure CPU-time consumed by the current thread, and counts events in a Recording to assert sampling rates.
Several tests declare or call nativeMethod to run busy loops; the native-like workload interacts with JVM sampling machinery to produce CPUTimeSample events observed by RecordingStream handlers.

TestFullStackTrace and TestCPUTimeSampleFullStackTrace are thin runners that invoke the BaseTestFullStackTrace harness in separate VMs to exercise ExecutionSample and CPUTimeSample full-stack capture respectively.
notable_relationships: These tests depend on the JVM's JFR implementation and sampling internals; changes to JFR event names, attribute semantics, recording APIs, or VM sampling thresholds can break tests across this folder.

Native workload expectations imply dependency on test-native libraries or native stubs provided elsewhere in the test tree or test harness — Java-only edits may be insufficient to keep tests functional.
JTReg harness and test execution environment (including JVM flags and image used) affect test outcomes; the folder assumes tests run under jtreg with access to RecordingStream and JFR functionality.
Platform differences (OS scheduler, JFR support, and ThreadMXBean CPU-time availability) influence test applicability and stability; some tests may be inherently platform-sensitive.
recommendations: Preserve timing/topology assumptions: do not alter throttle values, sleep durations, or recursion depth semantics without validating effects on sampling and stack assertions under realistic CI loads.

When changing signatures or moving classes referenced by nativeMethod declarations, ensure corresponding native implementations or test harness artifacts remain consistent and are available during jtreg runs.

Run these tests via jtreg and validate on the same CI-target platforms (Linux/macOS/Windows and architectures) because behavior is platform-dependent; run the relevant JFR and ThreadMXBean-dependent tests under configurations that expose CPU-time measurement.
Maintain RecordingStream lifecycle semantics: verify that closing and reopening recordings still triggers expected native sampling behavior when making edits that touch recording/event handling code.

After edits, execute the profiling test subset (tests in this folder) and throttle-sensitive tests under both low and loaded conditions to detect regressions or increased flakiness; pay attention to CI job logs for timing-related failures.

src/java.desktop/unix/classes/sun/font.description: This directory implements the Unix/X11-specific font subsystem glue for java.desktop: native font representation, strike/scaler management, fontconfig-backed configuration, X11/XRender text renderers and platform encoding/charset support. It bridges JDK font abstractions to X11/libfontconfig/native scaler contexts and provides caching, encoding maps and native-resource lifecycle handling that are critical for correct text metrics and rendering on Unix/X11 platforms.
key_behaviors: Discover and configure platform fonts via libfontconfig or legacy X11 XLFD mappings and translate those results into JDK CompositeFont descriptors and cached fcinfo properties.
Represent and parse native X11/XLFD physical fonts and create FontStrike instances that use native scaler contexts and glyph image pointers for rendering and metrics.
Map Unicode code units to platform glyph identifiers using per-encoding XMap tables and CharsetEncoder-backed encoding logic, supporting many legacy X11 encodings.

Manage native glyph caches and upload/compose glyphs through the XRender pipeline (uploading glyph bitmaps, evicting by budget, batching ELT lists) and invoke native draw paths for direct X11 drawing.
Allocate, cache and dispose native resources (scaler contexts, glyph memory) with disposer hooks to ensure native memory is freed when strikes are GCed.

insights.title: Native scaler contexts and glyph memory must be freed predictably
