key_behaviors: Translation of JVM-level constructs into AArch64 LIR/assembly via C1 and C2 pipelines (LIR generation, LIR emission, macro assembler helpers).
Emission of AArch64 machine instructions and data (Assembler & MacroAssembler) including instruction sequences for allocation, locking, safepoints and calls into runtime stubs.
Management of frame layout, interpreter activation sizes and register/opcode mappings (FrameMap, AbstractInterpreter layout functions) to satisfy ABI and GC/runtime expectations.
Provision of platform utilities that affect memory access and endianness semantics used by bytecode handling and runtime helpers.
Creation and initialization of CPU-dependent runtime stubs and safepoint/entry stubs that interact with the HotSpot runtime and GC.

insights.title: Global symbol name collision (uabs -> g_uabs)
insights.problem: A function previously named uabs collides with a glibc symbol on some platforms, causing link or runtime ambiguity.
insights.root_cause: A short, common global symbol name used in emitted/native helpers conflicts with platform C library symbols.
insights.solution: Ensure the renamed/global-namespace-safe symbol (g_uabs) is used consistently across all call sites and declarations, and verify linkage succeeds on target AArch64 toolchains and C runtimes.

insights.title: Tight coupling of offsets and activation sizes to runtime
insights.problem: Frame layout sizes, activation layouts and register offsets are platform-specific constants; mismatches between headers and implementation lead to corruption at runtime or during GC/safepoint transitions.
insights.root_cause: Multiple files declare or rely on platform-specific offsets and sizes (AbstractInterpreter, c1_FrameMap, headers), and these values must agree with runtime expectations and assembly sequences.
insights.solution: Any change to offsets/sizes/activation layout must be reflected consistently in declarations, assembler emission, and runtime consumers; validate by rebuilding hotspot and running safepoint/GCTest/JIT tests on AArch64.

insights.title: C1 and C2 backend behavior must remain consistent where semantics overlap
insights.problem: Separate implementations for C1 and C2 (macroassemblers, code stubs, globals) can drift, causing behavioral differences in generated code or runtime interactions.
insights.root_cause: Distinct code paths (c1_* and c2_*) implement similar runtime sequences and rely on shared platform conventions but are maintained independently.
insights.solution: When editing code-generation, calling conventions, or helpers used by both tiers, ensure parallel updates in both c1 and c2 components and validate with both JIT tiers enabled in builds/tests.

insights.title: Platform byte utilities affect bytecode and native memory semantics
insights.problem: Incorrect handling of native endianness or byte operations in utilities (Bytes, get_native_u2, put_Java_u8) can produce wrong program behavior or corrupt data interpreted by other subsystems.
insights.root_cause: Low-level helpers are relied upon widely for reading/writing multi-byte JVM/Java representations; platform assumptions must be preserved.
insights.solution: Maintain correct semantics in endianness helpers and validate with bytecode tests and cross-arch comparisons; exercise interpreter and serialization/deserialization code paths in tests.

insights.title: Runtime stubs are ABI-sensitive and affect safepoint/entry behavior
insights.problem: Stubs that implement safepoint polls, entry barriers, or runtime calls must match calling conventions, stack layout and register usage; mismatches cause crashes or GC miscoordination.
insights.root_cause: Code stubs (C1/C2 code stubs, Runtime1/CompiledDirectCall stubs) emit assembly sequences tightly coupled to platform conventions and runtime expectations.
insights.solution: Respect calling conventions and register clobber lists documented in platform-specific headers; when changing stub emission, run safepoint, GC and JIT entry/exit tests on AArch64.

key_files.why: Core AArch64 assembler that emits instructions and data; central to all code generation and affected by symbol/linkage changes.
Generates LIR for the C1 JIT, mapping JVM ops to platform ops and interacting with frame layout and register allocation; changes impact generated code sequences.
Produces C2/server-side entry and safepoint stubs that the runtime relies on; sensitive to calling convention and safepoint semantics.
Implements register-to-op mappings and frame addressing used by C1 and by code emission; influences stack layout and live-value tracking.
Provides low-level byte and endianness helpers used by interpreter/bytecode handling; subtle bugs here affect correctness across the VM.

construct_relationships: Assembler (assembler_aarch64.cpp) is consumed by MacroAssembler implementations (c1_MacroAssembler_aarch64.cpp and c2_MacroAssembler_aarch64.hpp) to emit instruction sequences and data.
MacroAssembler and StubAssembler emit runtime stubs (c1_CodeStubs_aarch64.cpp, c2_CodeStubs_aarch64.cpp) used for safepoints, entry barriers, allocation and runtime calls.
FrameMap (c1_FrameMap_aarch64.cpp/hpp) provides register/opcode mappings and stack addressing used by the C1 LIRGenerator (c1_LIRGenerator_aarch64.cpp) and LIR assembler/emitter (c1_LIR_aarch64.cpp).

AbstractInterpreter activation layout functions (abstractInterpreter_aarch64.cpp) determine interpreter stack/activation sizes that must match expectations in frame maps, compiled stubs and runtime consumers.
Bytes/endianness helpers (bytes_aarch64.hpp) are used by bytecode handling (bytecodes_aarch64.cpp) and by any component reading/writing multi-byte Java/native values.
notable_relationships: These files are platform-specific implementations referenced by HotSpot core runtime and JIT subsystems elsewhere in src/hotspot; changes can break cross-platform invariants or require updates to shared headers.
Symbol naming and linkage (e.g., uabs -> g_uabs) may interact with system C libraries (glibc) and affect linking; symbol changes can require updates across the entire native codebase.
ABI/offset constants declared here must remain consistent with other HotSpot subsystems (GC, runtime, assembly helpers) and with any generated metadata consumed by other components or tools.
C1 and C2 backends are independent code paths but rely on the same platform conventions; changes in one may need corresponding verification in the other and in the runtime entry/exit logic.
Build system and tests (HotSpot native build, gtests, jtreg hotspot tests) exercise these files; CI runs on AArch64/macos-linux/windows cross-architectures may reveal platform-specific issues.
recommendations: When editing, preserve ABI, calling conventions, register clobber lists and declared offsets; update all related headers/implementations in lockstep.
If renaming global symbols (e.g., uabs -> g_uabs) ensure every declaration and call site across the native tree is updated and that the symbol does not collide with platform libraries.

Run full HotSpot native build for AArch64 targets and execute hotspot unit tests/gtests and relevant jtreg tiers (at least hotspot/jvm and interpreter/jit tests) after changes that affect codegen, frames, or stubs.
Verify both C1 and C2 code paths when modifying code generation or helpers used by both; changes to macros/assembler helpers must be validated with both JIT tiers enabled.
Exercise interpreter and bytecode-related tests when touching AbstractInterpreter or bytes/endianness helpers to ensure interpreter activation/layout and memory access semantics remain correct.

src/hotspot/cpu/arm.description: This folder contains the ARM-specific parts of the HotSpot backend: the assembler (generic and ARM32-specific), abstract interpreter helpers for stack/frame layouts, C1 and C2 macro assemblers and LIR generator pieces, frame map/register mappings, and runtime/code-stub emitters. It is responsible for encoding ARM machine instructions and ABI-level conventions used by JIT compilers, safepoints, object allocation, locking and exception handling — changes here directly affect generated code, runtime calling conventions, and stack layout required for GC, deoptimization and stack walking.
key_behaviors: Translate high-level JIT LIR and macro assembler operations into ARM machine-level instruction sequences using the Assembler primitives and ARM32-specific encodings.
Define and maintain frame layouts and register mappings used by the interpreter, C1/C2 compilers, deoptimization and stack walkers.
Emit runtime code stubs (allocation, safepoint polls, exception handlers) that integrate with Runtime1 and the VM calling conventions.
Provide operand/address encodings (including rotated immediates) and condition/Address abstractions that the rest of the backend relies on.
Implement lock/monitor, object allocation and array compare/equals fast paths in both C1 and C2 macro assemblers that must interoperate with the GC and runtime.

insights.title: ARM32 immediate/operand encoding is delicate
insights.problem: Immediate values and operand encodings (rotated immediates, Address::make_raw, AsmOperand initializers) are highly architecture-specific and use compact encodings that can easily become inconsistent.
insights.root_cause: ARM's instruction set imposes constraints (rotated-immediate formats, addressing modes) that require coordinated encoding logic in assembler primitives and consumers.
insights.solution: Treat assembler_arm_32.cpp/header functions as canonical: any change to immediate/address encoding must update all consumers (macro assemblers, LIR lowering) and be validated by code-generation/unit tests that exercise uncommon immediates and addressing modes.

insights.title: Frame map and abstract interpreter must remain consistent
insights.problem: FrameMap register mappings and AbstractInterpreter activation layout are relied upon by deoptimization, stack walkers, safepoints and exception handling; mismatches lead to incorrect stack unwinds or corrupted callee-saved registers.
insights.root_cause: Multiple components (AbstractInterpreter, FrameMap, macro assemblers, runtime stubs) encode assumptions about register usage and layout independently.
insights.solution: Maintain strict invariants: any change to register sets or frame layout requires coordinated updates to FrameMap, AbstractInterpreter helpers, LIR generator expectations, and the runtime call sites.

insights.title: Runtime stubs and generated code must observe calling conventions and safepoint protocols
insights.problem: Stubs emitted by c1_CodeStubs_arm.cpp and Runtime1 integration call sites depend on exact register/stack usage and safepoint poll semantics; divergence causes GC, exception or patching failures.
insights.root_cause: Tightly coupled assumptions between generated stub code and runtime runtime1/VM call_RT semantics.
insights.solution: When editing stub emission or call_RT usage, ensure emitted sequences preserve caller-saved/callee-saved registers, safepoint poll placement, and handle patching expectations; validate with safepoint/GC tests and runtime patching tests.

insights.title: C1 and C2 macro assemblers must behave consistently
insights.problem: C1 and C2 implementations provide overlapping functionality (locks, fast allocation, array compares) but live in separate files; inconsistent behavior can cause functional discrepancies between the two JITs.
insights.root_cause: Distinct implementations and optimizations for C1 vs C2 may diverge if not updated together.
insights.solution: Treat macro-ops (monitor enter/exit, allocation fast paths, char array equals) as behavioral contracts: changes to semantics or register conventions in one place likely require reviewing the other and corresponding tests to ensure parity.

key_files.why: Contains ARM32 operand/address/rotated-immediate encoding logic used by nearly all instruction emission code.
Initializes frame map and register-to-operand mappings that define ABI/frame layout for C1 and interpreter interactions.
Implements high-level sequences for frames, allocation and locking used by the C1 JIT; changes impact object layout and synchronization paths.
Emits safepoint, allocation and exception handling stubs that must interoperate with runtime and GC protocols.
Defines AsmCondition, Address and other assembler API elements that are the interface contract for all assembler consumers in this directory.

construct_relationships: Assembler primitives (assembler_arm.hpp / assembler_arm_32.cpp) provide low-level instruction emission and operand encoding used by C1/C2 macro assemblers (c1_MacroAssembler_arm.cpp, c2_MacroAssembler_arm.cpp).

FrameMap (c1_FrameMap_arm.cpp / .hpp) defines register and operand mappings consumed by LIRGenerator (c1_LIRGenerator_arm.hpp / c1_LIR_arm.cpp) and AbstractInterpreter (abstractInterpreter_arm.cpp) for stack layout and deoptimization.

LIRGenerator and LIR lowering (c1_LIRarm.cpp / c1_LIR_arm.cpp) emit LIR that macro assemblers lower into Assembler primitives, so changes in LIR operand expectations must match assembler operand encodings.
c1_CodeStubs_arm.cpp emits runtime stubs referenced by Runtime1::call_RT and Runtime1::generate_* in c1_Runtime1_arm.cpp; these link generated code with VM runtime behaviors (safepoints, patching).

C2 macro assembler helpers for fast_lock/fast_unlock and char_arrays_equals (c2_MacroAssembler_arm.cpp/.hpp) rely on the same Assembler and register conventions as C1; they must be consistent with C1 implementations.
notable_relationships: Upstream VM/runtime: emitted stubs and calling conventions must match VM Runtime1/HotSpot internal expectations (call_RT, patching, safepoint protocols) — changes affect GC, exception handling and deoptimization.

Cross-architecture parity: other cpu/*/ folders implement analogous constructs; behavioral or ABI changes here may require corresponding updates/testing across architectures to preserve consistent JIT behavior in multi-arch builds.

Build and packaging: modifications require rebuilding libjvm and images for ARM targets (or cross-compilation); CI jobs and platform-specific toolchains must be used to validate changes on real ARM hardware or cross-compile environments.
Tests: hotspot/gtests and jtreg hotspot tests (allocation, synchronization, safepoints, deoptimization) are the primary downstream consumers and must succeed to validate correctness.
recommendations: When editing, preserve assembler API contracts (AsmCondition, Address shapes, AsmOperand behavior) and keep assembler_arm_32.cpp as authoritative for encodings; run build to catch mismatches.
Any change to register sets, frame layout or calling conventions MUST be reconciled across FrameMap, AbstractInterpreter, macro assemblers (C1/C2), LIR generator and runtime stubs before committing.

Run a full hotspot libjvm rebuild for the target ARM variant and execute relevant tests: safepoint/GC tests, allocation/fast-path tests, monitor/lock tests, deoptimization/stack-walking tests (jtreg/hotspot/gtest as applicable).
Be cautious modifying allocation and safepoint stub emission — these interact with GC and patching; validate with runtime patching and GC stress tests.
If changing encodings or macros that differ between 32-bit and other ARM flavors, ensure platform-specific guards are correct and re-run cross-arch consistency checks and platform CI where available.

src/hotspot/cpu/ppc.description: This directory contains the PowerPC (PPC) backend of HotSpot: instruction emission primitives, macro-assembler helpers, C1/C2 compiler backend support (LIR, frame maps, stubs), code-buffer management and PPC-specific byte/endianness utilities. It implements the machine-dependent pieces that produce and lay out executable code, define ABI and activation layout for PPC, and provide platform-specific runtime stubs used by the VM and compilers.
key_behaviors: Translating intermediate representations (C1 LIR and C2 compiler outputs) into PPC machine code via macro-assembler and assembler primitives.
Defining PPC ABI, frame layout and register-to-stack mappings used by code generators, frame walkers and runtime entry/exit sequences.
Generating and emitting runtime code stubs (safepoint polls, range checks, exception throwing, predicate failures) including size and alignment constraints.
Managing code cache and emitted code buffers: initialization, bundle/flush and branch destination handling for emitted code.
Handling PPC-specific memory operations: unaligned access, endianness conversions and loading of constants/literals for emitted code.

insights.title: Activation and frame-layout assumptions are encoded in multiple components
insights.problem: Activation sizes, top-of-stack layout and offsets are computed in abstract interpreter helpers and consumed by frame maps, macro-assembler and LIR code; mismatch leads to incorrect frame walking, GC/register spills, and incorrect exception/return behavior.
insights.root_cause: Machine/ABI-dependent offsets and register mapping are defined locally for PPC (e.g., pd_* offsets, nof_reg_args, R*_opr constants) and used across C1/C2 and runtime stubs.
insights.solution: Any change to frame layout, ABI constants, or activation-size computations must be coordinated across abstractInterpreter_ppc.*, c1_FrameMap_ppc.*, macro-assembler code and any consumer of pd_* offsets to prevent inconsistencies.

insights.title: Stubs and emitted sequences have explicit size and alignment constraints
insights.problem: Code stubs (C1/C2 safepoint/overflow/range-check stubs) and direct-call/compiled-call sizes are relied on by callers and by inline patching; miscalculating max_size or emitted instruction sequences can break branches, inline patching and prolog/epilog assumptions.
insights.root_cause: Emitter code exposes stub emitters and exposes size bounds (e.g., to_interp_stub_size, max_size) that are used for reservation/patching and linking.
insights.solution: When modifying stub emitters, update any declared size constants and ensure branch/patch sites and callers are updated; be aware of alignment and bundle flush behaviors in codeBuffer_ppc.hpp.

insights.title: Byte-order and unaligned access are handled by PPC-specific utilities
insights.problem: PPC is big-endian on some platforms and requires careful handling of unaligned loads/stores; misuse causes incorrect constant materialization and data reads/writes in emitted code.
insights.root_cause: Bytes/unaligned helpers (Bytes, get_native_u2, put_native_u4) centralize endianness/unaligned behavior for emitted sequences and constant encoding.
insights.solution: Changes touching constant materialization, data patching, or direct memory access must consider these helpers; ensure emitted sequences that read/write runtime memory follow the same endianness/unaligned semantics.

insights.title: Parallel C1 and C2 backends duplicate platform-dependent logic
insights.problem: C1 and C2 implementations each contain their own macro-assembler support, globals and intrinsics; inconsistent updates cause divergent behavior between the two compilers (different calling conventions, intrinsics, or generated sequences).
insights.root_cause: Separate files implement C1 and C2 variants (c1_*.cpp/.hpp and c2_*.cpp/.hpp) and both reference global flags and pd_* constants.
insights.solution: Edits to semantics that affect calling conventions, intrinsics, or ABI must be reflected in both C1 and C2 code paths; global flags affecting backend behavior may need synchronized updates.

insights.title: Target-specific initialization is split across pd_init/pd_compiler2_init
insights.problem: Platform-specific initialization functions are invoked at various points; missing or reordered initialization can leave dispatch tables or per-compiler tables uninitialized causing miscompilation or crashes.
insights.root_cause: Files expose pd_init (C1/C2 headers) and Compile::pd_compiler2_init (c2_init_ppc.cpp) which must run before code generation or runtime stubs are used.
insights.solution: When changing or relying on initialization behavior, ensure the correct initialization functions are still invoked at the expected points and that any new platform tables are initialized in the same phase.

key_files.why: Low-level instruction emission primitives and helpers (load_const, branch handling) used by macro-assemblers and code stubs.
C1 macro-assembler implementation that builds frames, allocates objects, and emits runtime sequences relied on by the C1 LIR generator and stubs.
C2 macro-assembler that implements intrinsics and helpers for the optimizing compiler; changes here affect optimized code generation and intrinsics behavior.
Computes activation sizes and layout that define stack frame formats and interpreter/GC expectations for PPC.
Interface for code-cache buffers, initialization and bundle flush/branch handling used when emitting and patching generated code.

construct_relationships: AbstractInterpreter (abstractInterpreter_ppc.cpp) defines activation sizes/layout that FrameMap (c1_FrameMap_ppc.cpp/hpp) and MacroAssemblers (c1_MacroAssembler_ppc.cpp, c2_MacroAssembler_ppc.cpp) must obey for correct prolog/epilog and GC/register spill locations.

Assembler primitives (assembler_ppc.cpp) are used by MacroAssembler implementations in both C1 and C2 backends to produce concrete instruction sequences and to materialize constants (load_const) and branches (branch_destination).

LIR generation (c1_LIRGenerator_ppc.cpp and c1_LIR_ppc.cpp) emits operations that rely on LIR/Opr representations and frame mappings; those interact with the C1 macro-assembler to reserve space and emit call/return sequences.

Runtime and stub emitters (c1_CodeStubs_ppc.cpp, c2_CodeStubs_ppc.cpp, c1_Runtime1_ppc.cpp) produce small executable pieces that are allocated in/through the code buffer subsystem (codeBuffer_ppc.hpp) and must conform to size/alignment declarations used by callers.
Bytes/endianness utilities (bytes_ppc.hpp) are consumed by assembler and code-emission code for proper constant encoding, unaligned loads/stores and runtime patching formats.
notable_relationships: This PPC backend must remain consistent with higher-level HotSpot VM expectations (safepoints, GC, stack walking, calling conventions) defined elsewhere in the VM; changes here have downstream effects on runtime, GC, and interpreter modules.

ABI constants and pd_* offsets must match corresponding declarations used by non-arch-specific code and by other architectures' implementations to ensure cross-platform correctness and tests compatibility.

Global flags and behavior switches declared here (c1_globals_ppc.hpp, c2_globals_ppc.hpp) are read by build/config and runtime; altering defaults or semantics affects JVM startup and CI test matrices across platforms.

Produced machine code is consumed by dynamic patching, safepoint/GC mechanisms and by tools (debuggers, profilers); emitted code layout/size affects linker/patch sites and must stay compatible with runtime patching infrastructure.
recommendations: Preserve ABI constants, pd_* offsets and activation-layout calculations; if modifying, update all dependent files in this directory (C1 and C2) and any non-arch consumers that read these offsets.

When changing stub emitters or instruction sequences, update any associated size/max_size constants and verify branch/patch site assumptions; consider codeBuffer behavior for flush and bundle alignment.
Respect endianness and unaligned access semantics encapsulated by bytes_ppc.hpp when modifying constant materialization, literal pools or memory read/write helpers.
Keep C1 and C2 backend implementations consistent for calling conventions, intrinsics and global flag interpretations; changes to one backend may require mirrored updates to the other.
Ensure platform-specific initialization routines (pd_init, pd_compiler2_init) remain invoked in the expected order; check that any new per-platform tables are initialized at the same lifecycle point.

Run PPC-targeted build and runtime tests after changes: a full build of HotSpot for PPC, C1/C2 compiler smoke tests, safepoint/GC tests, and relevant jtreg tests that exercise compiled code, stubs and patching to detect size/alignment/ABI regressions.

src/hotspot/cpu/riscv.description: This folder contains the RISC-V backend of HotSpot's code-generation and C1 JIT subsystems: assembler primitives and relocation, platform-specific macroassembler and LIR (low-level IR) lowering, C1 frame-map and interpreter activation layout helpers, and a set of runtime stubs and code-emission points. It is the implementation surface that maps HotSpot VM calling conventions, stack/frame layout, and runtime stubs to RISC-V instruction encodings and relocation semantics, so correctness here directly affects generated code correctness, GC/stack-walking, and interoperability with VM runtime services.
key_behaviors: Mapping VM-level activations and interpreter frames into RISC-V stack layouts and offsets used by both interpreter and JITted code.
Lowering C1 LIR to RISC-V instructions via the MacroAssembler, including arithmetic, allocation, lock/unlock, and exception prologue/epilogue sequences.
Emitting platform-specific runtime stubs and code stubs (C1 code stubs) and registering/finalizing them with the VM CodeBuffer and runtime tables.
Assembler-level handling: immediate encoding checks, endian-safe memory I/O helpers, address/relocation handling and literal-pool support for position-independent code.
Arraycopy and intrinsic lowering: producing specialized sequences, parameter preparation and runtime calls that must obey calling conventions and stack layout.

insights.title: Frame offsets and activation layout are shared across multiple components
insights.problem: Frame layout constants and activation size calculations are referenced by AbstractInterpreter, FrameMap, MacroAssembler and runtime stubs; mismatches will break stack-walking, exception handling and calling conventions.
insights.root_cause: Multiple translation units implement or consume the same platform-dependent offsets and activation sizing logic (abstractInterpreter_riscv.cpp, c1_FrameMap_riscv.cpp, c1_Defs_riscv.hpp, MacroAssembler stubs).
insights.solution: Any edit that changes offsets, sizes or register save/restores must be synchronized across the frame-map, interpreter-activation logic, macroassembler stubs and header constants; ensure consistent rebuild and test of stack-walking, exception and GC-related code paths.

insights.title: Relocation and literal-address handling is central to correct code emission
insights.problem: Address representation, relocation entries and literal pool assertions are implemented here; incorrect handling can cause wrong addresses or broken PIC code.
insights.root_cause: assembler_riscv.cpp (and inline helpers) provides core methods (Address::Address, address_relocation, code_fill_byte) and immediate-range checks used by higher layers.
insights.solution: When changing instruction sequences, immediates or literal-pool placement, validate relocation generation and linking phases; rebuild and run tests that exercise stub finalization and cross-object code addresses.

insights.title: Immediate and operand-size helpers constrain generated sequences
insights.problem: Encoding range checks (is_simm5, is_simm6, is_simm12, is_uimm2) are used to select short/long encoding sequences; misclassification breaks emitted code.
insights.root_cause: Assembler inline helpers gate when to use particular RISC-V encodings and must match runtime expectations for sign/zero extension.
insights.solution: Any change to immediate handling or instruction selection must preserve the exact numeric ranges and the sign/zero extension semantics; update all consumers and run instruction-level tests.

insights.title: C1 code stubs, CompiledDirectCall and runtime calls must be consistent
insights.problem: Stubs emitted by C1 (code stubs, safepoint polls, counter overflow handlers, compiled-direct-call trampolines) must match CodeBuffer finalization and Runtime1 initialization conventions.
insights.root_cause: Multiple files here implement or reference stub emission and initialization (c1_CodeStubs_riscv.cpp, c1_LIR_riscv.cpp, c1_Runtime1_riscv.cpp).
insights.solution: When modifying stub prologues/epilogues or calling sequences, ensure CodeBuffer pd_finalize_stubs and Runtime1 initialization remain consistent; exercise JIT stub finalization and direct-call pathways in tests.

insights.title: Arraycopy lowering coordinates parameter setup, type checks and runtime fallbacks
insights.problem: Arraycopy lowering has many variants (fastpath, checks, checkcast, type checks) that interact with register usage and calling conventions; differences can cause memory-safety or correctness issues.
insights.root_cause: The arraycopy implementation splits logic across lowering, parameter preparation, store/load helpers and emitted runtime calls (c1_LIRAssembler_arraycopy_riscv.cpp and headers).
insights.solution: Maintain consistent register use, stack parameter layout and calling sequences between the prepare/store/load routines and any runtime helpers; run arraycopy-specific JTReg tests and stress tests after edits.

insights.title: Endian helpers are relied on for safe memory IO
insights.problem: Bytes::get_native_u2 and similar helpers are used for reading/writing multi-byte values; incorrect endianness handling corrupts emitted data or constants.
insights.root_cause: Platform-specific bytes helpers are located in this folder and assumed by assembler and literal-pool code.
insights.solution: Any changes touching multi-byte memory access must preserve the endianness semantics; validate with tests that inspect literal pools and emitted constant data.

key_files.why: Core assembler relocation and address/literal handling used by nearly all code emission and stub/link phases.
Implements high-level sequences for allocation, locking, prologue/epilogue and other primitives used by C1 code generation.
Translates LIR to machine-level constructs and coordinates with the MacroAssembler and FrameMap; central to JIT output correctness.
Implements mapping between LIR frame slots and machine frame layout; ties logical registers/slots to concrete offsets.
Provides interpreter activation sizing/layout used by both interpreter and compiled/interpreted-call bridges; affects stack-walking and exception handling.

construct_relationships: AbstractInterpreter::size_activation / layout_activation define activation sizes used by FrameMap::map_to_opr and by StubAssembler prologue/epilogue sequences.

Assembler inline helpers (is_simm5/is_simm12/etc.) are consulted by LIRAssembler and MacroAssembler to choose instruction encodings; assembler_riscv.* provides Address, relocation and code_fill utilities consumed across code emission.
C1_LIRAssembler emits code sequences by invoking C1_MacroAssembler routines (allocate_object, initialize_header, lock_object/unlock_object) to produce concrete instruction streams.

C1 code stubs (c1_CodeStubs_riscv.cpp) are emitted and then finalized via CodeBuffer::pd_finalize_stubs and initialized by Runtime1::initialize_pd; CompiledDirectCall uses emitted stubs to implement interpreter-call trampolines.

Arraycopy lowering routines (generic_arraycopy, arraycopy_prepare_params and store/load args) coordinate with MacroAssembler emitted sequences and runtime stub calls, sharing calling convention and register usage assumptions.
notable_relationships: These files must interoperate with VM-wide runtime classes (Runtime1, CodeBuffer, CompiledDirectCall, StubAssembler) defined elsewhere in HotSpot; changes here can break VM initialization, stub registration and calling conventions.

Offset and constant definitions must stay consistent with c1_Defs_riscv.hpp and with arch-agnostic callers in hotspot/c1 and other CPU backends; the RISC-V implementation must match the expectations in higher-level JIT infrastructure.

Assembler/relocation behavior here must be consistent with other arch backends and with the linker/finalizer paths used by the build system; tests that run only on RISC-V target need to be executed to validate changes.
This subtree is compiled only for the RISC-V target; changes will only be validated in RISC-V builds and CI configurations that include riscv platforms.
recommendations: Preserve ABI/calling-convention and stack-frame invariants: any change to prologues/epilogues, saved registers, or slot offsets must be mirrored across FrameMap, DTrace/GC stack-walking code paths, and header constants (c1_Defs_riscv.hpp).

When modifying assembler encoding/imm ranges, update all inline helpers and the codepaths that rely on them (LIR lowering, MacroAssembler sequences) and validate by rebuilding and running instruction-level tests.
If you change relocation, literal-pool or Address handling, run full code-stub finalization and linking scenarios; check emitted literal data with assembly dumps and run JIT stub tests.
Keep .hpp declarations and inline definitions in sync with .cpp implementations; modify both together and compile the RISC-V target to catch mismatches.
Be aware there is a duplicated c1_CodeStubs_riscv.cpp entry in the metadata — edits to code-stub logic may need to be applied to multiple compilation units if duplicates exist in the tree.

Run platform-specific validation: make hotspot (or make images when appropriate), then run C1/JIT-targeted tests (hotspot gtests and relevant jtreg tests such as arraycopy and safepoint/stub tests) on a RISC-V build to validate changes.

src/hotspot/cpu/s390.description: This folder contains the s390-specific parts of the HotSpot backend: assembler and instruction/byte utilities, C1 and C2 compiler backend hooks (LIR, FrameMap, MacroAssembler, linear scan allocator), interpreter frame layout helpers, code-buffer and code-cache platform hooks, compiledIC/interpreter glue, and runtime helpers such as compressed klass reservation. It encodes ABI, register layout, alignment, code generation and patching behavior that must match the VM runtime and GC expectations for the s390 port.
key_behaviors: Lowering Java bytecode/IR to s390 LIR and machine code (LIRGenerator -> LIR/operands -> MacroAssembler emission).
Frame and stack layout calculation for interpreter and compiled methods (AbstractInterpreter, FrameMap, MacroAssembler build_frame/verified_entry).
Register allocation and constraints for the C1 backend (LinearScan hooks, register cardinality, caller-save decisions, adjacent-reg requirements).
Platform-aware code emission, buffering and finalization (assembler, CodeBuffer hooks, flush_bundle, finalize stubs, cpu data management).
Runtime glue between compiled calls and the interpreter/stubs (CompiledIC direct-call stubs, relocations to interpreter, Runtime1 stub generation).
Platform resource/setup behaviors (compressed klass address-space reservation, default tuning parameters for C1/C2 code cache and background compilation).

insights.title: Frame/register layout and interpreter activation sizes are platform-encoded
insights.problem: Frame layouts, offsets and counts (register map, pd fields) are encoded in multiple places and are consumed by generated code and stub sequences.
insights.root_cause: Multiple components (AbstractInterpreter, FrameMap, MacroAssembler, assembler) must agree on offsets and register numbering for correct callee/caller saving and deoptimization/stack-walking.
insights.solution: Treat constants and layout helpers here as authoritative for s390; any change requires coordinated updates across assembler, FrameMap, MacroAssembler and any code that computes or assumes offsets (including stubs and relocations).

insights.title: Byte utilities encode platform unaligned access and native size semantics
insights.problem: s390 has specific endianness and supports/assumes particular semantics for unaligned loads/stores; incorrect byte helpers can corrupt data when the interpreter or stubs access words/longs.
insights.root_cause: Low-level routines (Bytes::get_native_u2, put_native_u8) are used by interpreter/assembler to read/write frame and constant data.
insights.solution: Respect the bytes_s390 implementations; ensure changes maintain endianness and unaligned access semantics and are synchronized with any changes in consumer code.

insights.title: CodeBuffer and stub finalization must preserve instruction cache coherency and relocation assumptions
insights.problem: Platform hooks for finalizing stubs and flushing bundles perform CPU-specific actions necessary for correctness; breaking these steps can lead to executing stale or partially-written code.
insights.root_cause: s390-specific code emission and bundling (flush_bundle, pd_finalize_stubs) plus CPU data structures are relied on by runtime for executable code correctness.
insights.solution: When modifying emitted code shapes, sizes, or relocation models, also consider CodeBuffer pd_initialize/pd_finalize_stubs and ensure caches/flush operations and relocation bookkeeping remain correct.

insights.title: CompiledIC and direct-call interpreter glue encode stub layouts and relocation sizes
insights.problem: CompiledDirectCall stubs and to-interpreter glue have size and relocation expectations used by JIT/linker/runtime patching.
insights.root_cause: Relocations, patch points, and expectation of stub sizes are used when switching between compiled and interpreted code (and when patching to/from interpreted mode).
insights.solution: Changes to call stubs or relocation handling must preserve or update size/relocation metadata and any consumers that compute offsets into stubs.

insights.title: MacroAssembler allocation and header initialization depend on VM object layout and GC interaction
insights.problem: C1 MacroAssembler contains allocate_object/array and header/body initialization sequences that must match VM header layout and GC expectations (concurrency, barriers).
insights.root_cause: Allocator sequences are hand-coded and platform-specific; object header/klass layout or GC protocol mismatch will break correctness/runtime safety.
insights.solution: Maintain tight coupling between MacroAssembler allocation implementation and VM object header definitions and GC write/barrier semantics; any change needs cross-checks with runtime GC and header definitions.

insights.title: C1/C2 global defaults are platform-tuned
insights.problem: Platform default values (CodeCache sizes, background compilation, inlining/intrinsics enablement) affect code generation and runtime behavior; altering them changes memory and performance characteristics of compiled code.
insights.root_cause: These settings are encoded in c1_globals_s390.hpp and c2_globals_s390.hpp and are assumed by the rest of the compiler and runtime.
insights.solution: Respect these defaults when changing code generation or resource use; any modification should keep coherence between global defaults and expected runtime resource availability.

key_files.why: Central code emission site for C1: builds frames, emits allocation/locking sequences, and produces code that must match VM object/header layout and calling conventions.
Implements the mapping between virtual frame slots and physical operands/registers for the C1 backend; changes affect stack layout and calling conventions.
Low-level assembler primitives and condition handling used across code emission paths; foundational for correct instruction encoding and branch/condition inversion.
Defines unaligned/endianness-aware byte accessors used by interpreter and stubs; critical for correct data layout handling on s390.
Platform-specific hooks for code buffer initialization/finalization and flush operations; responsible for ensuring emitted code is coherent and executable.

construct_relationships: AbstractInterpreter (abstractInterpreter_s390.cpp) computes interpreter activation sizes that must match FrameMap and MacroAssembler build_frame layouts.

FrameMap (c1_FrameMap_s390.cpp/hpp) provides slot-to-operand mappings consumed by LIRGenerator (c1_LIRGenerator_s390.cpp) and by the MacroAssembler when materializing frames and saving/restoring regs.
LIR/Opr helpers (c1_LIR_s390.cpp/hpp) expose operand/register typing used by the LinearScan allocator (c1_LinearScan_s390.hpp) and by the MacroAssembler emission routines.

MacroAssembler (c1_MacroAssembler_s390.cpp) emits allocation, locking and call sequences that must be relocatable by CodeBuffer hooks and compatible with CompiledDirectCall stubs (compiledIC_s390.cpp).

Assembler primitives (assembler_s390.cpp) and byte helpers (bytes_s390.hpp) are used by interpreter, stub generators (Runtime1 and Runtime1::generate_code_for), and by compiled IC glue to read/write data and encode instructions.
notable_relationships: This s390 subtree must remain consistent with VM-wide definitions of object headers, calling conventions and GC barrier protocols defined elsewhere in HotSpot; changes here can affect the runtime globally.

Several pieces are platform mirrors of other architectures (frame layout, assembler, code buffer hooks). Any cross-platform testing or upstream changes to canonical layouts must be reconciled with s390 implementations.
Code cache and compilation defaults here influence build and CI behavior; failing to account for these sizes can cause resource-related failures during image or test builds.
CompiledIC/interpreter glue and runtime stub generation interact with the hotspot runtime linker/relocator; changes may require full-image rebuilds and test runs to validate relocations and patching.
recommendations: Preserve ABI, calling convention and frame/layout invariants: when editing constants or layout code, update all consumers (FrameMap, MacroAssembler, assembler primitives, and any stubs) to keep consistency.
Respect s390 endianness and unaligned-access semantics: verify any change touching Bytes helpers, memory loads/stores, or data layout is correct for big-endian unaligned cases.

When modifying emitted code shapes (stub sizes, call sequences, or instruction encodings), ensure CodeBuffer finalization, relocation metadata and flush semantics remain correct and update any size/offset assumptions in CompiledIC and Runtime1 glue.
Account for GC and object header assumptions when changing allocate/initialize sequences in MacroAssembler: validate against VM header definitions and barrier invariants.

Test strategy after edits: perform a full rebuild of hotspot and affected JDK images, run HotSpot unit tests (gtest where applicable), and run relevant jtreg test tiers that exercise interpreter/jit transitions, allocation, locking, and code-patching.

Keep global C1/C2 defaults and platform tuning in mind: changes that increase code size or CPU usage may require re-evaluating CodeCache and background compilation settings in c1_globals_s390.hpp and c2_globals_s390.hpp.

src/hotspot/cpu/x86.description: This folder contains x86-specific HotSpot backend support: JIT code emission (C1/C2), macro-assembler helpers (allocation, locking), frame layout and register mappings, CPU initialization, erratum alignment, and low-level byte helpers. It encodes architecture assumptions (register set, endianness, ABI/offsets, and alignment) that other VM components and generated code depend on, so modifications here affect runtime correctness and generated machine code.
key_behaviors: Produce x86 machine code and runtime stubs for C1 (client) and C2 (server) JIT compilers, including safepoint checks, exception/range/division traps, allocation and monitor operations.
Define and enforce x86-specific frame layouts, register-to-frame mappings and activation sizes used by interpreters and JITs.
Initialize CPU-specific compiler state and register masks needed by the backends.
Detect and mitigate architecture errata (Intel JCC erratum) by adjusting code alignment and tagging affected machine nodes during emission.
Provide low-level helpers for endian-correct memory reads/writes and finalize code buffers/stub emission used by the runtime.

insights.title: Frame layout and offsets are architecture-specific and globally observed
insights.problem: Frame sizes, reserved argument sizes and offsets (used by interpreter, JITs and runtime call sites) are encoded here in multiple places.
insights.root_cause: FrameMap, AbstractInterpreter and related headers define concrete offsets and register mappings that other VM components assume.
insights.solution: Any edit that changes frame layout, register mapping or pd_* offsets must preserve ABI invariants or be coordinated with all consumers (interpreter, stubs, calling conventions). Failing to do so will break stack walking, safepoint/restart, and cross-component calls.

insights.title: x86 is treated as little-endian; byte helpers centralize this assumption
insights.problem: Byte-level reads/writes are implemented with x86 endianness in mind; other code relies on these helpers for portable access.
insights.root_cause: Bytes::get_native/put_native and Java-specific variants encode little-endian behavior.
insights.solution: Changes to these helpers must maintain little-endian semantics and the Java/native data layout expectations; altering semantics without updating all callers risks corrupting runtime structures and generated code data blobs.

insights.title: Stubs and macroassembler operations must integrate with VM safepoints and thread state
insights.problem: Stubs emitted here (safepoint poll, range checks, allocation, monitor enter/exit) cooperate with VM safepoint, GC and thread state protocols.
insights.root_cause: Emitters call into or arrange for runtime transitions and rely on hard-coded offsets and calling sequences agreed with the rest of HotSpot.
insights.solution: Maintain the calling/stack conventions and safepoint side-effects when editing emission logic; changes that alter instruction sequences, stack usage or saved registers must be vetted against safepoint and GC invariants.

insights.title: Intel JCC erratum handling influences emitted instruction alignment
insights.problem: Certain branches must be aligned or padded to avoid erratum-triggering patterns; the emitter tags and aligns code accordingly.
insights.root_cause: Hardware errata require software-level alignment fixes applied at code emission time (IntelJccErratum analysis and alignment).
insights.solution: Any changes that affect code layout, block boundaries, or alignment logic should preserve or appropriately update the erratum-tagging and alignment routines; otherwise generated code may be subtly incorrect or slower on affected CPUs.

insights.title: C1 and C2 components share some conventions but have separate globals and init paths
insights.problem: C1 and C2 both emit x86 code but use different files, globals and initialization sequences; inconsistency can lead to mismatches in generated code or behavior.
insights.root_cause: Separate code paths (c1_*, c2_*) encode similar semantics (stubs, allocation, safepoint) with different implementations and feature flags.
insights.solution: When making changes that affect semantics shared by both compilers (e.g., allocation sequence, safepoint semantics, register use), ensure both C1 and C2 behavior remain compatible or that consumers are updated in lockstep; changes to global flags/configuration need consistent initialization.

key_files.why: Implements allocation, object initialization and monitor (lock/unlock) code emitted by the C1 macroassembler; central to generated object operations.
Contains C1 runtime stubs for safepoint polls, range checks, div-by-zero, and allocation fallbacks that are invoked from generated C1 code.
Defines x86 frame layout and register-to-frame mapping used by the interpreter and C1 backend (affects stack/ABI).
Performs CPU-specific initialization for the C2 compiler backend, including register mask setup; critical for C2 register allocation and codegen correctness.
Implements detection and alignment mitigation for the Intel JCC erratum; directly impacts emitted code alignment and correctness/performance on affected CPUs.

construct_relationships: AbstractInterpreter (abstractInterpreter_x86.cpp) computes activation sizes and layouts consumed by FrameMap (c1_FrameMap_x86.cpp) and the interpreter/JIT stack unwinders.
C1 macroassembler emitters (c1_MacroAssembler_x86.cpp) produce sequences that C1 code stubs (c1_CodeStubs_x86.cpp) call into or that the runtime expects (e.g., allocation fallbacks).

C2 initialization (c2_init_x86.cpp) sets register masks and state used by the C2 backend; those masks influence node lowering and emitted code that may be further processed for Intel JCC erratum (c2_intelJccErratum_x86.cpp).
Bytes helpers (bytes_x86.hpp) provide architecture-correct memory access semantics used by codebuffer/stub finalization (codeBuffer_x86.cpp) and any emitted data blobs.
CodeBuffer finalization (codeBuffer_x86.cpp) and erratum alignment logic (c2_intelJccErratum_x86.cpp) interact to determine final code layout of stubs and compiled methods.
notable_relationships: Upstream VM components (runtime class layouts, object header definitions, calling conventions) are consumers of offsets and ABI choices encoded here; any change must remain compatible with src/hotspot/runtime and Java-level expectations.
Other CPU subdirectories (e.g., amd64, sparc) implement analogous logic—consistency matters where multi-arch tests or shared conventions are assumed.
Build system and platform selection will compile different files depending on target architecture; edits here affect x86 builds only but may affect cross-architecture test expectations.

JTReg and HotSpot test suites, as well as platform-specific gtests, exercise the stubs, allocation paths and alignment fixes implemented in these files; regressions are likely to be found by hotspot/gtests and jdk tests exercising allocation, monitors and safepoints.
recommendations: Preserve ABI, frame layout and calling convention semantics or update all dependent consumers (interpreter, runtime stubs, stack walkers) when changing offsets or register usage.
When adjusting code emission, ensure safepoint, GC and thread-state protocols are maintained; verify emitted sequences preserve saved registers and stack frame expectations.
If touching alignment or layout logic, verify Intel JCC erratum tagging and alignment paths remain correct; code layout changes can require re-validation of erratum mitigations.
Maintain little-endian behavior in byte helpers; any semantic change must be propagated to all callers and validated with data-driven tests.

After edits, rebuild the x86 target and run architecture-relevant test sets: hotspot gtests, C1/C2 compiler tests, allocation/monitor/safepoint JTReg tests and cross-arch consistency checks to detect ABI or codegen regressions.

src/hotspot/cpu/zero.description: This directory contains the Zero CPU port of HotSpot: a platform-neutral, interpreter-oriented set of stubs, frame/layout definitions, endianness helpers, and small code-buffer/patching hooks used when the VM is built without a native code generator. It matters because it defines the interpreter-visible ABI (frame layouts, activation sizes, register maps, continuation metadata, and stub sizes) and provides the minimal assembler/disassembler/codebuffer contracts other VM subsystems rely on when there is no native backend.
key_behaviors: Define and expose interpreter and activation layouts (frame sizes, field offsets, interpreter state) consumed by the interpreter and runtime for stack walking, GC maps and exception handling.

Provide no-op or minimal assembler and disassembler implementations and inline helpers so higher-level code (MacroAssembler/C2/C1 interface layers) can be compiled and linked against a non-native backend.
Offer endianness-aware read/write helpers (Bytes) so bytecode and binary data are interpreted consistently on the Zero port.
Provide stub generation and code-buffer hooks (downcall/linker, compiled IC to-interp stubs, codeBuffer pd hooks) used by runtime call/patching paths even when no machine-code emission is present.
Expose continuation and freeze/thaw placeholders and register-map update helpers used by continuation/VM frame manipulation and stack-walking logic.

insights.title: Interpreter-visible layouts are authoritative for stack-walking and GC
insights.problem: Multiple files define activation/frame layout and field naming for interpreter frames and continuation entries. Discrepancies can break GC, deoptimization, and stack walking.
insights.root_cause: Zero implements platform-neutral definitions rather than emitting machine-specific prologue/epilogue, so all runtime consumers depend on the hard-coded sizes and offsets here.
insights.solution: Treat the sizes/offsets/names in these files as an ABI contract; any change must maintain compatibility or be synchronized with all code that depends on frame layouts and register maps.

insights.title: Many assembler/disassembler/continuation functions are intentionally stubbed
insights.problem: These files contain no-op or placeholder implementations (assembler, disassembler, continuation freeze/thaw) which are relied on by other subsystems expecting a concrete implementation on native ports.
insights.root_cause: Zero is a portable interpreter port with no real instruction encoding; therefore machine-level logic is absent and represented as stubs.
insights.solution: Changes must preserve the observable behavior of these stubs (signatures, side-effects, return values and sizes). Do not introduce semantics those callers would expect only on native backends unless callers are adjusted in lock-step.

insights.title: Stub sizes and offsets are used by callers to compute patch locations
insights.problem: Files such as compiledIC_zero.cpp and codeBuffer_zero.hpp expose or depend on sizes and finalize hooks for stubs; mismatches cause incorrect patching and runtime errors.
insights.root_cause: Callers (call-site stubs, linkers, runtime patchers) compute offsets and rely on hard-coded or reported stub sizes from these implementations.
insights.solution: Any modification that affects emitted stub size or layout must be reflected in the corresponding size-querying functions and in all consumers that allocate or patch those stubs.

insights.title: Bytes helpers centralize endian conversions for Java/VM binary formats
insights.problem: Byte-order sensitive reads/writes are implemented here and used by interpreter and stub-encoding helpers; incorrect behavior will corrupt class data, constant pools, and relocation information.
insights.root_cause: Zero must work identically across host endianness using software readers/writers.
insights.solution: Preserve the semantics of get_native/get_Java helpers; ensure consistency with the JVM bytecode and constant pool semantics and with any code that relies on these conversions.

insights.title: Header-bound constructs must match signatures expected by other VM components
insights.problem: Headers like c2_MacroAssembler_zero.hpp and continuationEntry_zero.inline.hpp provide interfaces that compiler or runtime code will include; mismatches break builds or cause undefined behavior.
insights.root_cause: Zero exposes platform-specific PD (platform-dependent) types and inline helpers so higher-level subsystems compile generically.
insights.solution: Keep function signatures, types and inline helper behavior compatible with expectations from the compiler, interpreter and runtime layers; any API changes require coordinated updates in callers across the VM.

key_files.why: Implements the interpreter core and frame layout names/offsets that other runtime components (GC, stack walkers, exception handling) depend on.
Defines basic interpreter typing and activation sizing/layout logic used to compute frame sizes and activation metadata for interpreted frames.
Provides the Zero assembler stubs and MacroAssembler pd hooks; used by code that emits or patches stubs even when no native code is generated.
Contains code buffer lifecycle hooks and stub finalization hooks; callers rely on these for shared-stub support and patching behavior.
Generates downcall/linker stubs for foreign/native calls on Zero and interacts with object relocation helpers (pd_add_offset_to_oop).

construct_relationships: BytecodeInterpreter (bytecodeInterpreter_zero.cpp/hpp and inline) depends on AbstractInterpreter definitions for activation size and layout to compute interpreter frames and VM-visible activation metadata.

Assembler helpers (assembler_zero.cpp and assembler_zero.inline.hpp) expose pd_* hooks and register VM representations used by MacroAssembler call sites and C2/C1 interfaces; MacroAssembler inline helpers call into Register/FloatRegister::as_VMReg conversions.

CodeBuffer hooks (codeBuffer_zero.hpp) are invoked by stub-emitting code such as CompiledDirectCall (compiledIC_zero.cpp) and DowncallLinker to initialize/finalize stub memory and to advertise support for shared stubs.
ContinuationEntry and continuation helper inlines interact with continuation freeze/thaw stubs and update_register_map routines used by stack-walking and GC metadata updates.
Bytes utilities are used by interpreter and stub/linker code to read/write multi-byte values in a host-endian-agnostic way for Java binary structures and stub data.
notable_relationships: This subtree must remain compatible with interpreter/runtime code in src/hotspot/runtime, src/hotspot/interpreter and with the rest of the VM that assumes certain frame layouts and register mappings.

Headers here (e.g., c2_MacroAssembler_zero.hpp) are included by higher-level compiler code (C1/C2 paths) which expects platform-specific MacroAssembler PD symbols; changes affect compiler build and linking.
Stub-size/patching behavior influences other subsystems (compiled ICs, JVMTI, JNI downcalls, runtime patchers); changes can cascade into code that computes offsets and applies runtime patches.
Endianness helpers must stay consistent with Java classfile and VM binary conventions used elsewhere in the repository (class loader, constant pool parsing).
The zero port is used for builds where no native code backend is present; build configurations and CI that select the Zero port depend on these files for a successful build and runtime.
recommendations: Treat frame sizes, field names/offsets, register-map update behavior and stub-size query functions as ABI contracts—do not change them without updating all callers and the ABI consumers across the VM.

When editing stub-emission or code-buffer finalize hooks, verify that any change in reported stub sizes or alignment is reflected in consumers that allocate/patch stubs (CompiledDirectCall, DowncallLinker, runtime patchers).
Preserve the public signatures declared in headers (inline helpers and pd_* hooks); any signature change requires synchronized updates in compiler/interpreter/callers to avoid build breakage.
Do not alter endianness/read-write semantics in Bytes helpers without confirming compatibility with classfile parsing, constant-pool handling, and any code that serializes/deserializes VM data.

After changes, build the Zero port and run interpreter-related tests (build images, interpreter-heavy jtreg/gtests or the equivalent VM test tiers) and run any GC/stack-walking tests to ensure ABI and metadata consistency.

src/hotspot/os/linux.description: This folder contains Linux-specific OS integration for HotSpot: cgroup (v1/v2) detection and controllers, container resource queries, hugepage and memory mappings reporting, ELF/stack checks, and Linux OSThread and OS hooks. These sources bridge kernel and procfs semantics into VM runtime flags, resource accounting, diagnostics and thread abstractions — changes here directly affect startup configuration, memory/cpu limits, telemetry and runtime behavior on Linux/container platforms.
key_behaviors: Detect and select Linux cgroup subsystem (v1 vs v2) and expose CPU/memory constraints to the VM.
Query and interpret procfs/kernel interfaces for hugepages, THP, memory mappings (/proc/*/smaps) and malloc internals for diagnostics.
Provide Linux-specific OS APIs and thread representation used by the VM (os::Linux, OSThread).
Translate kernel-level features (noexecstack, madvise/hugemem) into HotSpot runtime flags and behavior.
Expose diagnostic commands (malloc_info) and mapping printers used by tooling and NMT (Native Memory Tracking).

insights.title: Dual cgroup v1/v2 support with factory selection
insights.problem: Linux distributions and container runtimes may expose either cgroup v1, v2, or a hybrid setup; incorrect detection leads to wrong resource limits or inability to read controllers.
insights.root_cause: Multiple coexisting cgroup APIs and varying controller names/indexing; need to abstract differences and choose implementation at runtime.
insights.solution: Keep a factory-based selection that probes controllers and exposes unified CgroupSubsystem/CgroupInfo interfaces; ensure callers use this abstraction rather than relying on v1/v2 specifics. Risk: altering controller probing or naming breaks container resource detection and startup-adaptive defaults.

insights.title: Resource limits used to set runtime defaults
insights.problem: CPU and memory limits discovered via cgroups or OSContainer affect defaults for compilers (C1/C2) and runtime flags; missed or inconsistent queries can misconfigure parallelism or garbage collector heuristics.
insights.root_cause: Multiple layers read processor_count, per-CPU shares, or memory_limit_in_bytes via cgroup utilities and OS container helpers; these values propagate into flags defined in globals headers.
insights.solution: Maintain consistent use of CgroupUtil/OSContainer APIs and honor fallback semantics when controllers are absent. Risk: changing query semantics without updating all consumers will lead to inconsistent runtime behavior.

insights.title: Hugepage and THP detection influences memory management
insights.problem: Incorrect detection of explicit hugepage support or Transparent Huge Pages (THP) can affect memory allocation paths and performance expectations.
insights.root_cause: Detection relies on kernel interfaces and filesystem indicators; behavior differs across kernels and distributions.
insights.solution: Centralize hugepage detection (HugePages class) and expose clear flags consumed by allocation code. Risk: modifying detection logic or its timing can alter startup memory layouts and should be validated for performance/regression.

insights.title: Procfs parsing used by diagnostics and NMT
insights.problem: Parsers for /proc/*/smaps, /proc/self/maps, and malloc_info are brittle to format changes and require careful error handling.
insights.root_cause: These utilities assume specific procfs formats and fields; kernel updates or container environments (minimal /proc) may deviate.
insights.solution: Parsing code must be defensive and expose clear fallback behavior; any change can affect NMT outputs and diagnostic commands consumed by tools. Risk: altering output formats or callers' expectations will break tooling that consumes these diagnostics.

insights.title: ELF executable stack and symbol demangling used for validation
insights.problem: ELF parsing is used to assert no-exec-stack requirements and to demangle symbols for diagnostics; incorrect handling can affect security checks or diagnostics clarity.
insights.root_cause: Reliance on ELF headers and linker-produced attributes; platform differences may present subtle variations.
insights.solution: Ensure consistent demangling and stack-exec detection logic and preserve ABI expectations for any public helpers. Risk: changing behavior may affect security posture or the content of logs/diagnostics.

insights.title: OSThread wraps Linux thread semantics required by VM
insights.problem: OSThread lifecycle, IDs and synchronization primitives are relied on throughout the VM and must remain stable and thread-safe.
insights.root_cause: Multiple VM components assume thread_id semantics, destructor behavior and start/stop synchronization via startThread_lock.
insights.solution: Preserve OSThread invariants and locking semantics; any modifications require careful review of callers and concurrency implications. Risk: subtle concurrency bugs or resource leaks if semantics change.

key_files.why: Central factory and selection logic that decides cgroup v1 vs v2 and routes queries to appropriate subsystem implementations.
Implementation of cgroup v2 controllers (CPU/memory) — changes here alter how resource limits are read on modern systems.
Container detection and memory_limit_in_bytes implementation used by higher-level VM components to adapt to container constraints.
Encapsulates hugepage and THP detection logic that influences allocation and performance-sensitive behavior.
Linux OS interface and kernel/version hooks referenced widely by the VM; serves as the integration point for platform-specific features.

construct_relationships: CgroupSubsystemFactory (cgroupSubsystem_linux.cpp) probes system state and instantiates either CgroupV1Subsystem or CgroupV2Subsystem implementations.
CgroupUtil helpers (cgroupUtil_linux.cpp) provide processor_count and controller adjustment utilities that are consumed by CgroupSubsystem implementations and by OSContainer for limit computations.
OSContainer (osContainer_linux.cpp/hpp) depends on CgroupSubsystem/CgroupUtil to compute container memory limits and expose them via memory_limit_in_bytes.
Globals headers (globals_linux.hpp, c1_globals_linux.hpp, c2_globals_linux.hpp) expose runtime flags and defaults that are informed by OS-level detections (cgroups, CPU count, hugepages).
HugePages detection (hugepages.cpp/hpp) informs memory allocation logic and is exposed through OS hooks declared in os_linux.hpp.
MemMapPrinter and ProcSmapsPrinter read procfs mappings and feed NMT/diagnostic outputs used by tooling; these rely on stable procfs parsing semantics provided by other Linux helpers.
ElfDecoder/ElfFile (decoder_linux.cpp) are used for executable stack checks and for symbol demangling used in diagnostics and logging.
notable_relationships: Changes here affect HotSpot startup defaults consumed by compiler components (c1/c2) and garbage collectors; compiler headers in c1/c2 rely on runtime flags defined in globals files.
Behaviors depend on kernel features and procfs; upstream changes in the Linux kernel, container runtimes (Docker, systemd, Kubernetes) or distribution packaging can alter runtime probe results.
Diagnostics and admin-facing commands (malloc_info jcmd, NMT outputs) are consumed by tooling outside hotspot — CI tests and external tools expect stable output formats.
Build and configure probes may affect which features are enabled; this subtree assumes presence of Linux-specific build targets and may be affected by cross-compile or non-Linux builds.
Tests in test/hotspot and system/container integration tests will be sensitive to semantic changes in resource detection and thread behavior.
recommendations: Preserve public header APIs, ABI and OSThread semantics; any signature or behavioral changes require adjusting all callers across the VM.
When modifying cgroup detection or controller logic, ensure both v1 and v2 paths remain supported and validate on hybrid/legacy container setups.
Be defensive when parsing /proc, smaps and ELF headers; maintain fallback behavior for missing or unexpected formats to avoid startup failures in constrained containers.
Run the HotSpot test suite (hotspot gtests), relevant jtreg container/resource-related tests and NMT/diagnostic tests after edits; validate on multiple kernel versions and container runtimes.
Respect interactions with global runtime flags (globals_linux.hpp and c1/c2 defaults) — changing resource-query semantics can alter defaults widely, so check consumers for consistency.
Consider concurrency and locking invariants around OSThread (startThread_lock, thread_id) — ensure thread lifecycle changes do not introduce races or leaks.
Validate performance-sensitive changes (hugepages detection, processor_count) with representative workloads to detect regressions in allocation or GC behavior.

src/hotspot/os/posix.description: This subtree implements the POSIX-specific OS abstractions used by HotSpot: signal handling and safefetch (fault recovery), thread- and VM-level synchronization primitives (mutexes, monitors, semaphores, park/parkers), suspend/resume and crash-protection scaffolding, the socket-based attach/listener protocol, and a small perf-memory backend. It centralizes the platform-dependent, low-level interactions with POSIX semantics that the rest of the VM relies on for safe asynchronous operations, thread coordination, debugging/attach, and sampling (JFR) behavior.
key_behaviors: Registering and managing POSIX signal handlers and providing JVM_RaiseSignal/JVM_RegisterSignal entry points for the VM.
Safe memory fetch/continuation: catching faults using signal handlers and longjmp/siglongjmp or static assembly continuations to implement safefetch primitives.
Thread synchronization primitives and wait/notify semantics (PlatformMutex/PlatformMonitor, semaphores, platform parking) used by VM threads and runtime services.
Suspend/resume state-machine for stopping and resuming threads under POSIX, coordinating with signals and synchronization primitives.
Per-thread crash protection for sampling (JFR) and other sensitive threads, using per-thread jump buffers and guarded call/restore semantics.
Socket-based attach listener and attach protocol handling for debugger/jcmd connections, implemented on POSIX sockets.

insights.title: Signal handlers are central to safefetch and must be async-signal-safe
insights.problem: Signal handlers used for safefetch, JVM signal entry points, and suspend/resume can run on arbitrary threads and contexts where many libc calls and heap allocations are unsafe.
insights.root_cause: POSIX signal handlers have strong restrictions on which functions are safe to call; several components here rely on handlers to perform control flow (jmp/longjmp) and minimal state updates.
insights.solution: Any code changes touching signal handlers, safefetch, or code invoked from those handlers must avoid non-async-signal-safe functions, heap allocations, locks, or C++ destructors; preserve minimal and reentrant-safe handler logic and ensure correct use of sigsetjmp/siglongjmp semantics.

insights.title: Platform differences for semaphore and other POSIX primitives
insights.problem: Some implementations are conditional/non-Apple-specific and may differ in behavior (timedwait semantics, named vs unnamed semaphores).
insights.root_cause: OS variants have different semaphore APIs and semantics; code contains separate implementations and wrappers to accommodate these differences.
insights.solution: When editing semaphore/park/parkers or perfMemory code, preserve interfaces expected by the rest of the VM and keep platform-specific fallbacks intact; be aware of Apple vs non-Apple behavior and the need to maintain the wrapper abstraction.

insights.title: Sigsetjmp/siglongjmp and static continuation handlers must align with thread/register state
insights.problem: Safefetch implementations (sigjmp and static assembly variants) perform control transfers and must restore registers and stack consistently for resumed execution.
insights.root_cause: Different safefetch variants rely on different mechanisms for saving/restoring state; mixing or changing one without coordinating others can corrupt execution context.
insights.solution: Changes to safefetch, jmpbuf layout, or handler names must preserve the ABI and calling conventions used by the VM and any assembly continuations; maintain consistent definitions between declarations and inline/implementation files.

insights.title: Mutex/monitor and suspend/resume interact tightly and can deadlock if invariants break
insights.problem: PlatformMutex/PlatformMonitor inline ops and suspend/resume state transitions are used throughout the VM; incorrect changes may create deadlocks or races during VM safepoints or thread suspension.
insights.root_cause: Low-level lock primitives are used by higher-level VM safepoint and thread-coordination logic; these primitives must maintain strong invariants about reentrancy, owner tracking, and ordering.
insights.solution: Respect existing lock semantics (ownership, recursive/non-recursive behavior, notify semantics) and ensure changes preserve atomicity, ordering and compatibility with suspend/resume state machine semantics.

insights.title: ThreadCrashProtection ties into JFR sampler and uses jump buffers per thread
insights.problem: The crash-protection wrapper installs per-thread protection and jump buffers; mis-coordinating its lifecycle or memory can leave sampler threads unprotected or cause incorrect longjmp behavior.
insights.root_cause: Crash protection relies on per-thread state and careful install/restore semantics to catch and recover from faults in sampling code.
insights.solution: When modifying crash-protection or sampling-related code paths, maintain proper initialization/teardown of per-thread jmpbuf state and ensure interaction with global signal handlers remains coherent.

insights.title: Forbidden/permitted function macros affect what can be used in sensitive contexts
insights.problem: Files provide wrappers to forbid or permit certain libc/C++ functions in contexts such as signal handlers; accidental use of forbidden functions in those contexts can cause subtle failures.
insights.root_cause: The codebase enforces strict rules about which functions are allowed in signal or low-level contexts through macros that affect warnings/compilation.
insights.solution: Respect the FORBID_C_FUNCTION/permit_forbidden_function macros and ensure that any code intended for signal/asynchronous contexts is guarded and compiled with appropriate pragmas and wrappers.

key_files.why: Central registration and entry points for POSIX signal handling used by the VM; changes here affect how signals are installed and raised across the subtree.
Implements safefetch using sigsetjmp/siglongjmp; tightly coupled to signal handlers and per-thread jmpbuf semantics for fault recovery.
POSIX semaphore implementation used by parking, perf, and other synchronization consumers; platform-specific behavior is encapsulated here.
Defines PlatformMutex/PlatformMonitor implementations and inline behaviors; foundational for VM locking and must remain consistent with runtime expectations.
Implements the socket-based attach protocol for debugger/jcmd attachment on POSIX; interacts with sockets and async events and is an external-facing service.

construct_relationships: jvm_posix.cpp registers POSIX signal handlers that safefetch implementations (safefetch_sigjmp.cpp and safefetch_static_posix.cpp) and ThreadCrashProtection rely on to catch faults and transfer control.
SafeFetch implementations use per-thread jmpbuf state provided/declared in ThreadCrashProtection and safefetch headers to implement fault-safe read semantics.

PlatformMutex/PlatformMonitor in mutex_posix.hpp and inline helpers in os_posix.inline.hpp are used by the suspend/resume state machine (suspendResume_posix.*) and by other synchronization consumers (park_posix, semaphore_posix).
Semaphore implementation (semaphore_posix.cpp/.hpp) is consumed by higher-level parking primitives (park_posix.hpp/PlatformParker) and by PerfMemory backing store coordination (perfMemory_posix.*).

Forbidden/permit-forbidden wrappers (forbiddenFunctions_posix.hpp, permitForbiddenFunctions_posix.hpp) are referenced by code that must enforce async-signal-safety (signal handlers, safefetch, crash-protection) to suppress or enable certain function usages.
notable_relationships: This POSIX subtree is depended on by runtime components in src/hotspot/runtime (thread, safepoint, JFR sampler) and by Java-level tooling that uses the attach protocol; changes propagate to VM behavior and tooling compatibility.
JFR sampler and other diagnostics (perfMemory) rely on crash-protection and perfMemory implementations here; modifications can affect telemetry, diagnostics, and debugging tests.

Platform differences (Linux vs BSD vs macOS) are represented here; changes can have downstream effects on cross-platform CI jobs and must be compatible with build-time feature detection in the top-level configure/make system.

Signal- and safefetch-related changes interact with assembly continuations and calling conventions used elsewhere in the HotSpot VM and may require alignment with native/arch-specific code under src/hotspot/os/<arch>.
recommendations: Do not call non-async-signal-safe functions, allocate memory, or take locks from signal handlers, safefetch handlers, or any code reachable from them; verify async-signal-safety for any function added to those codepaths.
Preserve ABI/calling-convention contracts: keep jmpbuf layout and names consistent between declarations and implementations and between C/C++ and any assembly continuations.
When editing inline/header/impl triads (os_posix.hpp, os_posix.inline.hpp, mutex_posix.hpp), update all related declarations/inline definitions together to avoid ODR/behavior mismatches.
Respect platform-specific differences (Apple vs non-Apple semaphore behavior) and maintain conditional implementations; test changes on all POSIX variants used in CI.

Run the native HotSpot test suites and relevant JTReg/native tests after changes: at minimum run tier1 hotspot tests, JFR/sampler tests, attach/protocol tests, and suspend/resume/threading tests on affected platforms.

Be cautious about global state and per-thread state lifecycles (ThreadCrashProtection, safefetch jmpbufs); ensure proper initialization/teardown to avoid leaving threads unprotected or handlers inconsistent.
If making changes that touch signal registration or handler behavior, coordinate with other OS/arch-specific code and update any dependent assembly continuations or platform-specific code paths.

src/hotspot/os/windows.description: This folder contains Windows-specific OS abstractions and integrations for the HotSpot VM: thread and synchronization primitives, event/parking primitives, dynamic wrappers for optional Windows system libraries, JVM/ JNI entry points and attach support, diagnostics helpers (symbol decoding and memory-map printing), and platform-specific defaults for compiler flags. These components adapt HotSpot core behavior to the Windows ABI and runtime environment and are relied upon by many VM subsystems for correct operation on Windows hosts.
key_behaviors: Provide Windows implementations of low-level threading, synchronization and parking primitives used by VM threads and monitors.
Expose and register Windows-specific JVM/JNI entry points and signal/interrupt mechanisms used by the VM and native clients.
Dynamically load optional Windows system libraries (PDH, IPHLPAPI) and provide safe fallbacks; expose perf/network data through thin wrappers.
Support JVMTI attach via a Windows pipe-based listener that coordinates attach requests into VM attach operations.
Offer diagnostics: symbol decoding/demangling and memory-map printing to aid debugging and crash analysis.
Declare Windows-specific forbidden-function mappings and provide C wrappers for selected forbidden APIs used elsewhere in the VM.

insights.title: Runtime optional-API wrappers
insights.problem: PDH and IP helper functionality is accessed via dynamic runtime loading and function pointers; improper initialization or missing DLLs must be handled gracefully.
