PEMDecoder/PEMEncoder/Pem/PEMRecord -> X509Factory/PKCS8Key: PEM and DER parsing/encoding utilities feed certificate and key factory code; X509Factory uses PEM parsing and interns parsed certificates; PKCS8Key parses private key encodings consumed by KeyFactory implementations (RSA/EC/XDH).

KeyFactory SPIs (ECKeyFactory, XDHKeyFactory, RSAKeyFactory) -> PKCS8Key and KeySpec: KeyFactory implementations translate encoded forms into provider-specific key objects and consistently zeroize temporary encoded material.
notable_relationships: VM/native dependency: ThreadSnapshot instances are created/populated by the HotSpot VM (native side). Java-side consumers must respect the VM contract (null snapshots, lifetime race) and any API changes require coordination with VM native code.

Platform-specific code: aix source under java.base/aix implements behavior that differs from generic Unix; changes must preserve platform feature detection and provider semantics across supported OSes.

Security provider coupling: PEM/PKCS#8/X.509 parsing and key factory SPI implementations are central to the provider framework; changes impact certificate/key parsing, interning, and JCA/JCE compatibility.

Module boundary: These sources live in java.base and jdk.internal packages — changes can affect many downstream modules and the runtime image; public API and classfile metadata (e.g., PreviewFeature annotation retention) are sensitive to modification.

Build & test scope: Alterations here require full java.base rebuild and execute security tests, jtreg test suites, and VM-facing diagnostic tests; platform-specific builds (AIX, macOS, Windows) may behave differently.
recommendations: Preserve public API semantics and classfile metadata (retention policies, PreviewFeature markers) when editing code in java.base; ensure ABI/source compatibility expectations are respected.

When modifying code that interacts with the VM or native methods (ThreadSnapshot.create, RandomAccessFile.open0, socket native integrations), verify the native contract and run platform-specific builds and VM tests.

Respect provider selection and classloading semantics: FileSystems relies on installed providers and system properties; do not change provider lookup behavior without checking provider-loading tests and subsystem integration.

For security-sensitive code, maintain zeroization of temporary byte arrays and avoid exposing raw key material; validate with security/unit tests that rely on deterministic clearing and encoding formats.
Validate thread-safety and null-handling: callers should defensively handle null ThreadSnapshot results and provider methods that may return null for unsupported features to avoid races and crashes.

Run a full relevant test matrix after edits: at minimum rebuild java.base, run jtreg security and nio tests, run test tiers exercising SSL/TLS handshakes, and execute VM diagnostic tests that use ThreadDumper. Include platform-specific test runs for AIX/Linux/macOS/Windows as applicable.
When changing caching/interning (X509Factory), consider memory and identity impacts: run tests that parse many certificates/CRLs and verify expected interning behavior.
Maintain PEM canonical semantics (line wrapping, CRLF, ISO_8859_1 outputs) and certificate/key parsing behavior; run interoperability tests that round-trip PEM/DER for certs and keys.

test.description: This subtree contains the jtreg and unit tests that exercise JVM runtime features, with a heavy focus on Java Flight Recorder (JFR) profiling events, HotSpot diagnostics (thread dumps, CDS), and a smattering of security and vectorization tests. These tests both validate VM behavior (native sampling, throttling, eliminated locks, CDS/AOT flags) and provide shared test utilities (event name constants, stack-trace harnesses) that other tests rely on. Test correctness depends on JVM internals, timing/threshold behavior, RecordingStream lifecycle, and stable output formats from the VM.
key_behaviors: Configure and enable JFR event types (CPUTimeSample, ExecutionSample) via Recording / RecordingStream, then block until an event is observed and the stream is closed.
Drive workload threads (busy loops, recursive call chains, native-method loops) to provoke sampling and collect profiling events for analysis.
Measure and assert sampling rates and throttling using thread CPU-time (ThreadMXBean) rather than wall-clock time where robustness is required.
Validate captured stack traces and truncation/depth semantics using a shared harness that spawns recurse/worker threads and inspects recorded event stacks.
Produce and parse HotSpot diagnostic outputs (plain and JSON thread dumps) to detect VM optimizations (e.g., eliminated locks) and compare runtime-provided event names against test coverage.

insights.title: Avoid wall-clock reliance for sampling rate assertions
insights.problem: Tests that used wall-clock time for sampling-rate assertions experienced intermittent failures under variable system load and scheduling.
insights.root_cause: Sampling and scheduling are influenced by platform load; wall-clock intervals are not robust for verifying CPU-sampling behavior.
insights.solution: Use thread CPU-time (ThreadMXBean) or other CPU-time based measurements to make assertions resilient to external load. Recognize tests that still depend on internal VM thresholds (e.g., naked_short_sleep) and treat them as sensitive to VM timing semantics.

insights.title: Centralized event name constants
insights.problem: Hard-coded JFR event name strings across tests make maintenance error-prone and risk divergence from runtime event identifiers.
insights.root_cause: Multiple tests reference the same runtime event identifiers in-line rather than from a single authoritative source.
insights.solution: Tests import canonical event name constants from test/lib/jdk/test/lib/jfr/EventNames.java; changes to event identifiers or namespaces must be reflected there to keep tests in sync.

insights.title: Tests parse VM diagnostic outputs
insights.problem: Tests parse HotSpot thread dumps (plain and JSON) and fail if the dump format or semantic labeling changes.
insights.root_cause: Parsing logic relies on specific formatting and reported attributes (e.g., eliminated lock indicators) that come from VM diagnostics.
insights.solution: Any edits that alter thread-dump formatting, JSON fields, or eliminated-lock messaging will likely break parsing tests; maintain compatibility or update affected tests accordingly.

insights.title: Profiling tests depend on native sampling and VM thresholds
insights.problem: Many profiling tests exercise native sampling and internal VM thresholds (throttles, sleep thresholds); small VM changes can change observable behavior.
insights.root_cause: Tests trigger and assert on VM-internal behavior (native CPU sampling, scalar replacement evidence, CDS/AOT flags) that is not purely Java-level.
insights.solution: Recognize that modifications to HotSpot sampling logic, related native code, or VM flag defaults impact these tests; when modifying runtime behavior, update tests and test harness expectations or safeguard via flags.

insights.title: Test coverage scanner depends on test tree contents
insights.problem: TestLookForUntestedEvents scans the test tree for event names and compares against EventNames; moving files or renaming tests can change coverage results and cause false positives.
insights.root_cause: The scanner uses textual search across test sources and a canonical EventNames mapping to infer coverage.
insights.solution: Keep test identifiers discoverable in the source tree, and update EventNames or scanner exclusions when reorganizing test files or intentionally omitting coverage for specific events.

key_files.why: Primary test validating CPUTimeSample throttling logic; uses ThreadMXBean-based CPU-time measurements to assert sampling rates and is sensitive to scheduling and sampling configuration.

Shared harness for validating full-stack capture semantics across profiling tests; it spawns worker threads, collects recordings, and asserts stack contents — many profiling tests depend on its behavior.
Centralized source of JFR event name constants used by tests; changing event identifiers or categories requires corresponding updates here to keep tests consistent.
Validates VM-reported eliminated-lock evidence via thread-dump parsing (plain and JSON); tightly coupled to diagnostics output format and optimization reporting.
Scans runtime event names against tests and EventNames to find untested events; sensitive to test tree layout and string references in tests.

construct_relationships: BaseTestFullStackTrace spawns recurse/worker threads (using RecursiveMethods) and uses Recording/RecordingStream to capture profiling events, then inspects event stack traces to validate order, depth, and truncation.

Profiling tests (TestCPUTimeSample*, TestFullStackTrace, TestCPUTimeSampleNative, etc.) enable JFR event types (CPUTimeSample, ExecutionSample) and rely on RecordingStream lifecycle (enable event -> wait for event -> close stream) to terminate test runs.
TestCPUTimeSampleThrottling measures CPU-time via ThreadMXBean and counts JFR CPUTimeSample events in a Recording to assert throttle behavior without relying on wall-clock timing.
DumpThreadsWithEliminatedLock invokes HotSpotDiagnosticMXBean.dumpThreads and parses the produced plain/text or JSON dumps to detect scalar replacement or eliminated-lock indicators.
TestLookForUntestedEvents queries the runtime for non-experimental JFR event names and cross-references them against test sources and the EventNames constants class to detect missing test coverage.
notable_relationships: Many tests depend on HotSpot native behavior (native sampling, scalar replacement, CDS/AOT flags); changes in src/hotspot or VM flag defaults can change test outcomes.
JFR tests depend on the JFR runtime module shipped with the JDK — changes to event definitions, names, categories, or default attributes in the runtime must be reflected in EventNames and tests.

Some tests call native methods or expect native-like busy loops; these require that native support and test harnesses provided by the build/test environment are available (jtreg, built VM with JFR enabled).
Thread-dump parsing tests assume stable diagnostic output formats (plain and JSON); cross-cutting changes in HotSpot diagnostic formatting are upstream risks to these tests.
The test coverage scanner (TestLookForUntestedEvents) is sensitive to source layout: renaming/moving test files or changing the way tests reference event names will affect its results.
recommendations: When editing tests or related utilities, run the jtreg test subset that covers JFR profiling, HotSpot diagnostics, and affected hotspot jtreg tests locally (or CI) to detect regressions; ensure JFR is enabled in the test VM configuration.

Respect the shared contracts: do not change event name strings, Diagnostic dump JSON field names, or RecordingStream lifecycle semantics without also updating EventNames.java, parsing logic, and dependent tests.

Be mindful of timing sensitivity: prefer CPU-time based assertions where used; if changing any timing/throttling behavior in the VM or tests, expect flakiness and rerun tests under varied load and multiple iterations.

Account for native dependencies: tests that reference native methods or rely on HotSpot internals require a built VM with the relevant native capabilities; edits that change native signatures or expectations must be synchronized with native test helpers.

If reorganizing or renaming test files, update TestLookForUntestedEvents expectations and EventNames mappings to avoid false positives in coverage scanning; keep textual references to event names discoverable by the scanner.

..description: This top-level src subtree (dominated by java.base) implements core runtime services including low-level I/O, filesystem provider selection (including AIX specialization), networking, locale and font helpers, VM-facing diagnostics (thread snapshots/dumps), and extensive security/crypto parsing and factories (PEM/PKCS#8/X.509 and KeyFactory implementations). These files mediate between Java public APIs, provider/SPIs, and VM/native contracts, so changes here affect platform behavior, security semantics, public API expectations and VM integration.
key_behaviors: Platform-specific provider selection and adaptation: mediates generic API callers to concrete FileSystemProviders (default and AIX-specialized) and honors system properties that can change provider chaining.
Low-level I/O and native integration: open/read/write semantics, FileDescriptor lifecycle and cleanup, FileChannel binding, and VM/native contracts (native open0, ThreadSnapshot.create).

Security object encoding/decoding and factory translation: PEM/DER parsing and encoding, PKCS#8 handling, X.509 parsing/interning and KeyFactory translations that produce provider-specific key objects.
Diagnostics and VM tooling: VM-populated ThreadSnapshot instances are consumed by ThreadDumper to produce textual/JSON dumps; these flows must tolerate transient thread lifecycles and file errors.
Networking and runtime compatibility: socket I/O integrates NIO, poller/virtual-thread logic and legacy socket semantics (EOF/connection reset emulation).

insights.title: FileAttributeView availability must reflect FileStore support
insights.problem: Files.getFileAttributeView could return a UserDefinedFileAttributeView even when the underlying FileStore did not support the user view, producing unusable views and potential crashes or user confusion.
insights.root_cause: Platform-specific provider returned an implementation without verifying store capabilities; callers assume non-null view is usable.
insights.solution: Provider implementations should return null when a FileStore does not support a requested attribute view; code that adapts Unix provider behavior must query the store capability before constructing/returning a view.

insights.title: Temporary encoded key material must be cleared
insights.problem: Encoded/derived key bytes and derived SecretKey instances were exposed or left uncleared (e.g., using getEncoded(), constructing SecretKeySpec without clearing), increasing window for sensitive-data leakage.
insights.root_cause: Conversion and KDF helper usage created transient byte[]/SecretKey objects whose lifecycle was not consistently zeroized across all code paths.
insights.solution: Consistently zeroize temporary byte arrays and clear/overwrite SecretKey material where possible after use; favor APIs/constructs that centralize clearing and be mindful of intermediate getEncoded() calls that return new byte arrays.

insights.title: Thread snapshot generation is transient and can fail
insights.problem: Diagnostics code attempted to dump threads even if the VM-created snapshot was missing (e.g., thread terminated during snapshot), leading to null dereferences or misleading output.
insights.root_cause: Caller assumptions that ThreadSnapshot.of always returns a snapshot; VM/native create(thread) can return null if snapshot could not be created.
insights.solution: Consumers must defensively handle null snapshots and terminated threads when building dumps; snapshot factories should normalize return values (canonical empty arrays) and be explicit about null semantics.

insights.title: Default FileSystem provider chaining and discovery must be preserved
insights.problem: Provider selection and defaulting is sensitive to system properties and installed provider list; changes can alter which provider is considered default or how newFileSystem is delegated.
insights.root_cause: FileSystems mediates provider discovery and honors a DefaultFileSystemProvider property; platform-specific providers extend shared base classes and rely on installedProviders ordering.
insights.solution: Any edits must preserve the provider discovery/order semantics and respect the DefaultFileSystemProvider system property and installedProviders list; platform-specific code should defer to the UnixFileSystemProvider for non-specialized behavior.

insights.title: File descriptor and channel lifecycle must be coordinated
insights.problem: RandomAccessFile integrates a lazily-created FileChannel and FileDescriptor cleanup; inconsistent lifecycle handling could leave descriptors open or double-close.
insights.root_cause: Shared descriptor accessed by both RandomAccessFile methods and FileChannelImpl; finalization/cleanable registration and native close paths must be coherent.
insights.solution: Maintain a single definitive descriptor lifecycle owner, register cleanup exactly once, and ensure channel creation returns an object bound to the same descriptor without duplicating close responsibilities.

insights.title: Handshake message ordering and secret lifecycle in TLS
insights.problem: Finished message processing could proceed while other handshake consumers (e.g., EncryptedExtensions) were still pending, and derived secrets were created via older helpers that required manual clearing.
insights.root_cause: Handshake consumer/producer ordering assumptions and mixed KDF usage led to potential ordering races and inconsistent secret zeroization.
insights.solution: Handshake processing must verify ordering constraints before transitioning cipher state; derived secrets must be produced and cleared using the defined KDF API and avoid exposing raw encoded key bytes.

key_files.why: Central factory for default and non-default FileSystem instances and mediator for provider discovery and default-provider chaining; changes here affect which FileSystemProvider is used globally.
Low-level legacy I/O entrypoint that creates/uses native descriptors, integrates with FileChannel and FileDescriptor cleanup and JFR tracing; edits affect descriptor lifecycle and I/O semantics.
Produces VM-facing thread dumps (text/JSON) consumed by diagnostics and tooling; tightly coupled to VM-supplied ThreadSnapshot instances and file/byte-array output semantics.
Core internal representation and parsing/encoding of PKCS#8 private keys; impacts how private key bytes are parsed, canonicalized, cached and cleared and affects KeyFactory translations.
Immutable thread-safe decoder used by many security subsystems (certs, keys, CRLs); changes influence parsing behavior and interoperability with X509Factory, PEMRecord and PEMEncoder consumers.

construct_relationships: FileSystems locates FileSystem instances by querying installed FileSystemProvider implementations; AixFileSystemProvider extends UnixFileSystemProvider and is returned by FileSystems when the provider list/order or default property indicates AIX usage.

RandomAccessFile opens native descriptors via native open0 and lazily constructs a FileChannel (FileChannelImpl.open) bound to the same FileDescriptor; both sides must coordinate close/cleanup behavior and JFR event emission.

ThreadDumper calls ThreadSnapshot.of(Thread) to obtain VM-supplied snapshots; ThreadSnapshot instances are produced by a native create(Thread) bridge and map VM ordinals to Java enums for locks/blockers that ThreadDumper serializes.

PEMDecoder/PEMEncoder/Pem/PEMRecord form a PEM parsing/encoding layer consumed by X509Factory and PKCS8Key for certificate, CRL and private-key parsing; KeyFactory implementations (ECKeyFactory, RSAKeyFactory, XDHKeyFactory) take parsed encodings (often via PKCS8Key) to produce provider-specific Key objects.

Finished (TLS handshake) uses KDF/VerifyData generation and interacts with session/handshake state transitions; it produces/consumes derived secrets and must coordinate ordering with other handshake consumers (EncryptedExtensions) and ensure secrets are cleared after use.
notable_relationships: Many classes here depend on native/VM contracts (RandomAccessFile.open0, ThreadSnapshot.create, NioSocketImpl native socket operations); edits to Java-side signatures or expected behaviors may require corresponding native changes in HotSpot.

Security parsing and key factory code are consumed by higher-level APIs (java.security, crypto providers) and tests; changes affect interop with provider implementations and external encoded artifacts (PEM/DER/PKCS#8).

Build and test flows (make/configure, JTReg tests) exercised by CI rely on preserved behavior; platform-specific code (aix folder) ties to runtime platform flags determined at configure/build time (make, make/PreInit.gmk).

JFR event emission and diagnostics (ThreadDumper output, JFR FileRead/FileWrite events) are relied on by monitoring/test harnesses; altering event boundaries or semantics can break tests and tooling expectations.
recommendations: Preserve native/VM contracts: do not change method signatures or expected null semantics for native-bridged factories (e.g., ThreadSnapshot.create, RandomAccessFile.open0) without coordinating corresponding native changes and updating tests.

Respect security lifecycle constraints: ensure temporary byte arrays, derived keys, and SecretKey/SecretKeySpec usages are cleared consistently across success and error paths; maintain existing zeroization and serialization (KeyRep) behaviors.

Maintain provider discovery semantics: keep FileSystems' provider ordering and DefaultFileSystemProvider property handling intact; platform-specific providers should continue to defer to UnixFileSystemProvider for non-specialized behavior.

Coordinate descriptor/channel ownership: when modifying RandomAccessFile or FileChannel creation/close paths, ensure a single authoritative cleanup registration and run file/descriptor lifecycle tests to avoid leaks or double-close races.

Handle transient thread/VM state defensively: ThreadDumper and consumers of ThreadSnapshot must tolerate null/missing snapshots and threads terminating during snapshot creation; run HotSpot diagnostic/thread dump tests after edits.

Run the appropriate test suites after edits: at minimum build images and run relevant jtreg/unit tests for filesystem, networking (NIO sockets), security (PEM/PKCS#8/X.509, KeyFactory), TLS handshake tests, JFR and VM diagnostic tests (test-tier1 plus targeted security/diagnostic tests).

Be cautious about API/ABI stability: changes that affect public classes, serialization (KeyRep), annotation retention (PreviewFeature), or provider SPI behaviors can impact downstream code and must preserve backward compatibility or be coordinated with compatibility processes.
